(1831-1900)

REPORT

BY FR. AMBROGIO ESZER, O. P.

GENERAL RELATOR

pp. 1–2

1.1. The iter of the Cause of the Servant of God Anna Rosa Gattorno (1831-1900) has been long and troubled. The Servant of God had founded a great Congregation which, already at the time of the Foundress's death, was carrying out a vast charitable and apostolic activity on an intercontinental scale. Just 13 years after her passing the Roman Ordinary Process was begun (1913-1927), while the first Rogatorial Process, that of Naples (1912-1918), was already under way. Three other Rogatorial Processes were held in Palermo (1913-1927), Piacenza (1912-1922) and Genoa (1917-1919), the native city of the Servant of God. In these processes 118 witnesses and 7 co-witnesses testified, 125 witnesses in all, among whom were: 2 Cardinals, 1 Archbishop, 8 canons, 4 monsignors, 3 other secular priests, 1 Capuchin, 1 Piarist and 1 Priest of the Mission, 84 sisters of the Congregation of the Daughters of Saint Anne, 12 «lay» women and 8 lay men. As can be seen, the Daughters of Saint Anne make up a good 64.4% of the entire body of witnesses.

pp. 2–3

1.2. Dwelling a little longer on the Tabella Index Testium et Summarii, we can see that the 7 co-witnesses were able to testify very little or nothing at all, so much so that their depositions are statistically almost non-existent. It is therefore more truthful and realistic to assume the number of 118 witnesses. With respect to this number, in the two cases in which a co-witness had said something, we removed his deposition from the count of the depositions of the 118 witnesses, but the difference is negligible. As regards the individual Questions, on «de ortu, patria et parentibus» of the Servant of God, 12 of the 125 or 118 witnesses respectively were able to testify (9.6% or 10.1%); «de Servae Dei vita saeculari», 16 (12.8% or 13.5%); «de Servae Dei vita religiosa et vocatione», 19 (15.2% or 16.1%); «de virtutibus in genere», 27 (21.6% or 22.9%); «de fide heroica», 28 (22.4% or 23.7%); «de spe heroica», 25 (20% or 21.2%); «de heroica caritate erga Deum», 25 (20% or 21.2%); «de heroica caritate erga proximum», 32 (25.6% or 27.1%); «de heroica prudentia», 34 (27.2% or 28.8%); «de heroica iustitia», 31 (24.8% or 26.2%); «de heroica fortitudine», 25 (20% or 21.2%); «de heroica temperantia», 23 (18.4% or 19.4%); «de heroica paupertate», 19 (15.2% or 16.1%); «de heroica oboedientia», 15 (12% or 12.7%); «de heroica castitate», 19 (15.2% or 16.1%); «de heroica humilitate», 19 (15.2% or 16.1%); «de Donis supernis», 15 (12% or 12.7%); «de pretioso obitu», 13 (10.4% or 12%)1; «de fama sanctitatis», 32 (25.6% or 27.1%); as well as «de gratiis et miris», 9 (7.2%), that is, 8 (6.7%)2. On all 20 questions of the Tabella Index, an average of 21.9% of the 125 witnesses (17.5%) or, respectively, 21.8 of the 118 witnesses (18.4%) were able to testify. This result highlights the fact that the Servant of God possessed a religiously very rich personality, but one hard for other people to approach. Although this does not show an excessive knowledge on the part of the witnesses, it does indicate that they testified very freely, without being influenced by the Actors. The points of gravity in the spiritual life of the Servant of God that most obviously impressed the witnesses are her heroic charity toward neighbor (32, which make 25.6% and 27.1% respectively), her heroic prudence (34, which make 27.2% or 28.8% respectively) and her heroic justice (31, which correspond to 24.8% or 26.2%).

1.3. As we have already said, the Servant of God does not present herself to us as a simple figure: she was, indeed, a most devout woman but, both because of her somewhat severe and reserved character, which did not open easily to the people around her, and because of the events of her life and her painful experiences, it was not always easy to enter into the spiritual intimacy of her soul. Nevertheless, as a wife and mother of a family, she will today be close to those many faithful who hope to see fathers and mothers of families raised to the altars. But the marriage of the Servant of God was a Calvary, not because she did not love her husband, but because of the misfortunes that struck him and, as a consequence, his family. The kinsfolk of our Servant of God stood, politically and religiously, on opposite shores. The Congregation she founded was to be one of those chosen instruments to halt the religious devastation and secularization of the Italian people, carried out by anticlericals, liberals and Freemasons. On the other hand, the Servant of God, a woman in the world but not of the world, of vast horizons, could not remain insensitive to the religious needs of other countries, across the ocean. Meanwhile, it is not surprising that a woman so determined and so deeply Christian should become the target of attacks by the Evil One and his satellites, who are always to be found, even in the Church. She was accused of being thirsty for power, greedy for money, psychically unbalanced, etc. For this reason we had to request some researches and expert evaluations which, although they had not been drawn up at an earlier time, were carried out under our supervision and then approved. Special mention is due to Rev. Sister Roberta, archivist of the Mother House of the Daughters of Saint Anne, because with immense diligence and equal competence she assisted the work of the Very Rev. Fr. Postulator and external Collaborator, Fr. Carlo Lizarraga, C.P., in the composition of the Summarium and in the drafting of the Informatio of the Cause, carried out with his usual mastery.

2.1.1. In the Summarium we find all the depositions of any importance, coming from the various Processes. Great care has been taken in compiling the so-called cappelli (introductory summaries), which inform more than exhaustively about the procedural setting of the depositions and about the witnesses themselves.

pp. 3–4

2.1.2. The Interrogatoria follow, very useful for seeing which question the witnesses were answering in their depositions, as well as an equally useful prosopography of persons who had some importance in the events of the Servant of God's life.

2.2.1. In the second part of the Summarium, expressly introduced by an index, documents concerning the Servant of God are collected and grouped in sections A-H, which are, moreover, listed again and briefly commented on in chapter I, b) of the Informatio. In section G, particular attention is deserved by the vote of the Very Rev. Fr. Paolino Zavarella, O.F.M., on the state of normality of the Servant of God (pp. 859 ff.), the graphological report on her personality (pp. 894 ff.) by Sante Bidoli, as well as some documents relating to the «Dilata» of the Holy Office. In section H there stands out the extract from the book «Spiritual Profile of Rosa Gattorno, Foundress of the Congregation of the Daughters of Saint Anne» by Fr. Làzaro Iriarte, O.F.M. Cap., a renowned specialist in the doctrine of the spiritual life and Consultor of this Congregation (pp. 934-1057).

2.2. It is precisely the above-mentioned expert evaluations that have swept away certain objections, both against the character and against the penances of the Servant of God. But it must also be pointed out that the mysticism of suffering is a characteristic of nineteenth-century Catholicism and of the first decades of the twentieth century. On the one hand the existence of residual ascetical (but not dogmatic) elements of Jansenism cannot be denied, but much more important seems to be the fact that during the above-mentioned period a process of separation of culture from the Christian religion was taking place, which created in many religious souls a real agony whose true cause they were, perhaps, not fully aware of. This separation was an immense evil from which the Church, the living body of Christ on earth, had to suffer. And it is clear that chosen souls such as that of our Servant of God felt the longing to share in those sufferings and to unite themselves, through their own suffering, more closely with Christ, in His Church. Thus the general and painful depression in the face of the ruin of the unity between culture and religion could acquire a new meaning. Today even Religious adapt easily to a completely de-Christianized and secularized civilization, but it is not said that this is truly an ideal state and one inevitably wonders whether it is not often the fruit of a certain frivolity that has nothing to do with the metanoia, that is, the penance or conversion, that marks the conduct of our Servant of God and is the condition of the conversion of the world.

p. 5

3.1. The Informatio, drawn up by the Very Rev. Fr. Postulator and external Collaborator, begins with a useful biographical sketch of the Servant of God and continues with a brief look at the evidentiary apparatus. There follows, in chap. II, an excellent description of the era in which the Servant of God lived, which is based above all on the expert report of Gabriella Airaldi: The Historical-Environmental Humus of Genoa, from the Mid-Eighteenth Century to the Birth of Rosa Gattorno, found on pp. 917-934 of the Summarium. But the said Postulator widens his gaze to the whole socio-political evolution in Italy, bringing out the involvement of close relatives of the Servant of God in that national movement of the Risorgimento, which led immediately to the first attempts at colonial policy. With the example of the Congregation of the Daughters of Saint Anne it becomes clear once again how incapable the nationalist-liberal-Masonic State was of solving the problems of social and hospital assistance for the needy, so that it was forced to call upon the collaboration of fervent Catholics, who on other occasions were the target of furious «anticlerical» propaganda and of measures of suppression on a national scale. As a result, in November 1886, the Daughters of Saint Anne had to take over the direction of the hospital at Assab in Eritrea, «soon extending their activity inland for the benefit of the native population»3. Also well done is the chapter on the Three Great Popes in the Time of the Servant of God, which puts in a fine light the filial love of our heroine for the successor of Saint Peter, as well as her healthy obedience to the supreme ruler of the Church. Indeed, she founded «her» Congregation in collaboration with the Church, which did not diminish but broadened and stabilized her creativity. The Informatio continues, in its chap. III4, with a substantial account of the life of the Servant of God, followed by the customary description of her heroic virtues and her charisms.

pp. 5–6

3.2. Particular attention is deserved by chap. VIII of the Informatio5, which resolves some difficulties concerning the complaints about the administration (of the Servant of God), the relationship with her son-in-law Barbiellini and his family, the question of Fr. Tornatore, co-Founder of the Congregation, the Apostolic Visitation, the contrary witnesses, as well as the question of the «Dilata». The Informatio closes with chap. IX, on the reputation for holiness and miracles6. And, in the Conclusion, the Very Rev. Postulator is concerned to state: «At the end, therefore, of the examination of the whole picture of Mother Rosa Gattorno's conduct as a young woman in her family, as a wife, as a mother, as a widow and then, finally, as foundress and religious superior general, the final and overall judgment can only be positive and flattering: the Servant of God was a heroine in the exercise of all the virtues»7.

4. Therefore, having studied all the Acts of this Cause and all the historical sources pertaining to it, we have become convinced that no further supplementary studies are necessary, considering that the material presented is more than sufficient for the Very Rev. Theological Consultors to examine it for the purpose of their vote on the heroicity of the virtues and the reputation for holiness of the Servant of God Anna Rosa Gattorno.

Feast of Saint Francis of Assisi

MOST EMINENT CARDINALS, MOST REVEREND CONSULTORS,

1. — The earthly life of the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno, whose life I am about to outline and whose extraordinary holiness, exercise of the virtues and exceptional flowering of charisms I intend to bring to light, is wholly wrapped in an aura of privilege and abundance of grace. To appraise adequately the singular spiritual — and also human — richness of this singular figure of our time in Italy, one must use, so to speak, the spectacles of the supernatural, since it is all too evident that it was God who worked in her and through her authentic wonders of grace and heavenly sublimity. It is undeniable, indeed, that the Lord «has looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid» (Lk 1:48) and has done great things in her, according to the divine style of all time.

Fortunately, we are very well informed about every aspect of her life's course, which has been described to us by eyewitnesses, often well qualified, so as to carry out the necessary study in depth of the various aspects of the personality of Mother Rosa Gattorno, and also to be certain that certain phenomena that occurred in her must be taken seriously, placed within the context of her special call to the experience of the divine, and therefore interpreted as being of supernatural origin.

In the present Informatio we shall give a summary presentation of the era and the course of the life of Mother Rosa Gattorno, then prepare a reasoned Synthesis of her virtues and her charisms, and then bring out her reputation for holiness in life and after death up to the present moment. All this is preceded by an illustration of the sources of information.

2. — First, for a panoramic overview, it is fitting to prepare the following

BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCH

1831, 14 October: the Servant of God is born in Genoa in the parish of Our Lady of the Vineyards and is baptized the same day in the parish of St. Donatus, the second of six children, with the name Rosa Maria Benedetta.

1843, 19 April: she is confirmed.

1850: she assists her maternal grandmother in her last illness, showing a particular aptitude for caring for the sick.

1852, April: she moves with her family to Via Scurreria, near the cathedral of St. Lawrence.

1852, 5 November: she marries Gerolamo Custo.

1852, 6 November: the newlyweds leave for Marseilles, where financial ruin awaits them; they are taken back into the home of Rosa's father, in Genoa.

1853, 8 December: Carlotta is born. At a tender age the little girl becomes deaf-mute.

About 1854: she begins daily Communion.

1855, 28 November: Alessandro is born at Sampierdarena.

About 1856: Rosa and Gerolamo settle in the parish of St. Syrus (Genoa). Rosa makes a vow of perpetual fasting. Gerolamo goes to work in Russia with his brother-in-law Federico.

She takes the cord of St. Francis as a tertiary.

1861, 8 December: she makes a vow of poverty.

About 1862: she receives the gift of a singular participation in the Passion of the Lord, suffering its pains in her hands, feet and heart, above all on Fridays.

1864, February: the Servant of God Giuseppe Frassinetti asks her to accept the presidency in Genoa of the Daughters of Mary. She feels inspired to found a new religious congregation.

CHAP. I
THE EVIDENTIARY APPARATUS

As we shall have occasion to show, after the death of the Servant of God spontaneous and convinced manifestations occurred, an unmistakable sign of a truly popular reputation for holiness. From that moment on this reputation not only knew no interruption but kept growing, so that in 1912 the Process was begun, and was then carried out with complete regularity in all its different phases:

a) The testimonial proofs.

3. — The canonical Processes regularly conducted number five in all, four Rogatorial Processes being added to the Roman Ordinary Process; the total number of witnesses examined is very high, as many as 118 and 6 co-witnesses, of whom 116 de visu and only 2 de auditu a videntibus.

These Processes are:

— A. Roman Ordinary Process, held from 1913 to 1927 to examine 43 witnesses, 12 of them ex officio; all but one were direct witnesses and only one indirect. Among those who gave their deposition are counted two Cardinals, one Archbishop, five Monsignors, two Priests, twenty-six Religious women, and eight lay persons, among them a Princess.

— B. Neapolitan Rogatorial Process, held in the years 1912-1918, to examine 31 witnesses of whom 2 ex officio and 4 co-witnesses; all are de visu and, as regards their distribution by category, three Monsignors, one Priest, seventeen Religious women and one lay person testified.

— C. Additional Process of Diano, conducted in 1917 to examine a Monsignor and a religious co-witness, both de visu.

— D. Palermo Rogatorial Process, conducted in 1913-1927 to hear 18 witnesses of whom 2 ex officio and all de visu. As regards their distribution by category, one Monsignor, one Priest and sixteen Religious women testified.

— E. Piacenza Rogatorial Process, carried out in 1913-1922, to hear 28 witnesses of whom 3 ex officio and all but one de visu. The testimony was offered by 2 Monsignors, 2 Priests, 19 Religious women and 4 lay persons.

— F. Genoa Rogatorial Process. This Process, held in 1917-1919 in the Servant of God's diocese of origin, took into consideration 9 witnesses and 2 co-witnesses, all de visu. Among them testified one Monsignor, three Religious women and six lay persons.

In view of the description of the Processes just given, we can only praise the diligence of the Actors for having carried their zeal to the point of tracking down every possible witness who had concrete evidence to offer. The good results achieved will be set out, at least in part, in the outline of the life of the Servant of God, but they will be far more evident in the treatment of the main theme of the present Informatio: namely, the examination of the virtues in general and in particular, as well as the examination of the reputation for holiness before and after death.

b) The documentary proofs.

4. — Under letter A, there are the personal documents that make it possible to certify the salient phases of the life of the Servant of God from birth to death. Then, from letter B to the end of the Summarium, there are documents suited to shed light on particular problems, often connected with the requests for clarification put forward by the Very Rev. Relator of the Cause.

— Under letter B, there are documents concerning the genesis and development of the religious vocation of the Servant of God and the subsequent foundation of the Daughters of Saint Anne, begun and brought to a good end by the Servant of God herself.

— Under letter C, we group several documents concerning the first Rules and Constitutions of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

— Under letter D, we present a selection of precious documents illustrating the relationship of the Servant of God with the Barbiellini family, a source of so much sorrow for Mother Rosa Gattorno.

— Under letter E, we offer a necessary synthesis of those documents that will best help us understand the role and place of Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, Priest of the Mission, at the side of Mother Gattorno at the beginning of the foundation.

— Under letter F, we group the documents concerning the Apostolic Visitation imposed on the Institute before the Servant of God died.

— Under letter G, the judgments of the Theological Censors on the writings of Mother Rosa are reported. Besides the two customary ones, we also have: the vote of the Very Rev. Fr. Paolino Zavarella, O. F. M., on the state of normality of the Servant of God and the graphological study of the personality of the same Servant of God, written by Prof. Sante Bidoli of S. Donà di Piave (Venice).

— Under this same letter G are gathered some documents that clarify the painful affair of the Dilata imposed by the Holy Office, which caused the halting of the Process for many years, but which finally reached a happy conclusion on 3 April 1979.

— Finally, under letter H, as a conclusion to the whole documentary section, we present two studies of evident value:

1. The first on the historical environment of Genoa, from the mid-eighteenth century to the birth of Rosa Gattorno. The author of this study is Gabriella Airaldi, lecturer in Medieval History at the University of Genoa.

2. The second is an extract from the book Spiritual Profile of Rosa Gattorno, Foundress of the Daughters of Saint Anne. The author, the Very Rev. Fr. Làzaro Iriarte, O. F. M. Cap., Consultor of our Congregation for the Causes of Saints, studies as a master the human, spiritual and mystical life of the Servant of God and offers most valuable clarifications, for example on the aspect of her life of penance united to the mystery of Christ the Redeemer.

CHAP. II
THE ERA IN WHICH THE SERVANT OF GOD LIVED

a) Political and social aspects in Italy.

5. — The Servant of God Rosa Gattorno was born in the city of Genoa on 14 October 1831, at a historical moment when the Restoration in Italy was already feeling the ferment of the Risorgimento.

After the defeat of Napoleon, the Congress of Vienna had arranged Italy into seven States: the Kingdom of Sardinia, the Lombardy-Venetia Kingdom united to Austria, the Duchy of Parma and Piacenza, the Duchy of Modena, the Grand Duchy of Tuscany, the Papal States, the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. At the death of the Servant of God, on 6 May 1900, Italy was not only unified under the House of Savoy but had also sought expansion in Africa.

The nineteenth century presents itself as a very complex period, both because of the redefinition of the States and because of the transformation of society, the gradual awakening to the rights of man — and of the worker in particular —, and the birth of industry. These indications help us understand the complex psychological adaptation that the Servant of God, together with her contemporaries, also had to make. But this was not what constituted a problem: as a believer and devoted daughter of the Church she felt suffering and distress at the way Italian unification was being brought about and at the use that part of the social forces made of progress and unity against the Catholic religion. The process of political unification, in fact, brought with it fratricidal struggles, bloodshed, the rise of enmities within towns and even within families.

Within the Italy of the Restoration and then of the Risorgimento, Genoa holds a singular place. The ancient maritime Republic, which had known centuries of prosperity and splendor, had seen its importance gradually decline and at the end of the eighteenth century had lost its independence; yet precisely when the city became a province of Napoleon's empire, its aristocratic ruling class, widened to include the band of professional economic and cultural operators, was transformed along modern lines. The loss of political autonomy did not cause excessive regret, because the entrepreneurial ruling class found interesting outlets and a market for incoming and outgoing trade, thanks to the port, with ever wider horizons8.

All this was put at risk after the Congress of Vienna by the annexation to Piedmont, which Genoa tried in every way to resist, but its fate was sealed, and the situation from 1815 onward was anything but rosy: heavy taxes were feared to maintain the Savoy Court and the large army, and the bureaucratic and backward system was criticized. Around 1830 the conditions matured for an economic recovery and Genoa became an economic, but also political and social, «laboratory»9.

6. — In the period of the struggle for national unity, Genoa truly presents itself as a driving center. G. Oreste puts it this way, drawing a picture of Genoa in the Risorgimento:

«The components of this complex picture are numerous: democrats (Mazzinian and not), socialists, moderates and constitutionalists, economists and men of culture, aristocrats, legitimists, religious and conservative clericals, backward and reactionary clericals, progressive clericals, educators and pedagogues, women's circles and salons, humorists and polemicists, ordinary people, humble workers, professionals, theater circles: it is a whole variegated world, rich in fertile vitality, engaged in one way or another in the problems of the moment with a liveliness and a fundamental seriousness that make Genoa one of the most important centers of our Risorgimento and, I would add, also one of the most decisive»10.

Against the background of this variegated world, the Servant of God did not enter directly into political movements as such, except by engaging and offering her witness of faith to the Mazzinians and Garibaldians who frequented her house. She was concerned above all with the concrete problems of the sick, the poor, abandoned girls, and those struck by epidemics. Her action fits into the long tradition of Genoese society, in which women had a singular role, notably different from that in other peoples and other States, and this since the Middle Ages. G. Airaldi writes:

«Because of the absence of the man (father, husband, brother, sons, relatives) far away at sea, the woman must of necessity face important problems of daily life [...]. There is — and this element remains a precise constant — a constant mobilization of volunteer work, even within the great families. Genoese noblewomen unite — while remaining wives and mothers — to intervene on behalf of those who suffer, generally victims of epidemics, famines, poverty and chronic illness [...]. The charitable and hospital vein will be a precise leitmotif of the social history of Genoa, with a constant presence of women (especially of high social standing) always accompanied by support for/from the Church»11.

7. — Between 1820 and 1831 the Genoese Giuseppe Mazzini followed the Carboneria movement, which fueled various insurrections in different Italian cities. Mazzini then began to work on his own, founding Young Italy in Marseilles, nurturing the ideal of a united Italy in the form of a republic. The maternal uncle of the Servant of God, Federico Campanella, an intimate friend of Giuseppe Mazzini, set up the Genoese Committee of the new association, together with the brothers Jacopo and Giovanni Ruffini, working very actively to spread that institution and preparing an insurrection that was to break out in Genoa in the first months of 1833. The plot, however, was discovered: some patriots were executed, others held in prison. Federico Campanella escaped capture by taking refuge in the Gattorno house and managed to find shelter in France.

The failure of the Carbonari insurrections first and the Mazzinian ones afterward strengthened the desire to achieve the unity of Italy through a confederation of States on the model of the German Confederation, and especially that of North America. The neo-Guelphs, among them Vincenzo Gioberti, were oriented toward a confederation of States under the patronage of the Pope. The Piedmontese moderates, among them Cesare Balbo and Massimo D'Azeglio, proposed a confederation of States under the King of Sardinia. There was no lack of republican federalists. These currents did not reach the vast majority of the people12.

p. 11

In 1846, with the election of Pius IX to the pontificate, the neo-Guelph program seemed about to be realized, since the first acts of the new Pope, interpreted in a liberal sense, fed exaggerated hopes and expectations. In 1848 all of Europe was swept by a revolutionary wave that affected Italy, Germany, France and Austria. The grave events between 1843 and 1853 and the failures of the unitary idea caused the federalist project to fade and attention to turn more and more toward the Kingdom of Sardinia and the House of Savoy.

The opportunity seized by Cavour to bring Piedmont into the game of the European powers was the Crimean War: he agreed to send a contingent alongside the Anglo-French against Russia on condition that Piedmont take part as a formal ally. He was thus able to raise the Italian question at the Congress of Paris in 1856 and force it on Europe's attention. In May 1860 Giuseppe Garibaldi, having gathered about a thousand volunteers, landed in Sicily and quickly conquered it, then moved up the peninsula as far as Naples. The brother of the Servant of God, Federico Gattorno, also took part in the Expedition of the Thousand; being in Russia because of his business and having heard of the enterprise, he fitted out a ship at his own expense, gathered 150 Italian volunteers and went to join the Garibaldians.

8. — In the summer of 1860 almost all of Italy was under the Savoy monarchy: the territory of the present provinces of Rome and Viterbo remained part of the Papal States because Napoleon III guaranteed their existence, but the fate of the papal possessions was sealed. On 14 March 1861, Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed King of Italy; national unification, however, was not peaceful; the extension of the Piedmontese system of government to the southern regions took no account of the different social and environmental conditions and provoked understandable discontent; moreover, many partisans offered armed resistance that the Piedmontese government labeled «brigandage», whereas in reality the partisans were fighting for their legitimate sovereign. Count Solaro Della Margarita, a member of the government under King Charles Albert, wrote in 1860 about the plebiscites that were meant to appear as a spontaneous phenomenon while being carried out with arms:

p. 12

«The despoiling of the Pope, whether by revolt of his subjects or by aggression of a foreign power, is as condemnable as any other despoiling that violates the rights of any other independent and legitimate Prince»13.

9. — In 1866 the law suppressing the religious Orders was extended to the whole Kingdom of Italy: ecclesiastical property was confiscated and sold off. In this very year the Servant of God courageously carried out the foundation of her Institute in the city of Piacenza. In 1870 the conflict between Prussia and France allowed the Italian government to occupy what remained of the Papal States and Rome itself. Politically, the radical change in the Italian situation was accomplished. Rome, by the plebiscite of 2 October 1870, was annexed to united Italy and on 30 June 1871 became its capital.

The Servant of God lived through these events with deep suffering, not so much because of the political events in themselves as because of the opposition and violent hostility toward religion and the Apostolic See that they revealed. To this was added the suffering for her brother Federico, who took an active part in that hostility and in that same year was still fighting under Garibaldi's orders on French soil, earning the rank of colonel in the Garibaldian army.

The thirty years from 1870 to the early 1900s were undoubtedly a period of crisis for the Kingdom of Italy. In this period, in line with European foreign policy, Italy too attempted its colonial expansion. In 1882 the base of Assab was acquired; in 1885 Massawa was occupied; in 1890 the Eritrean colony was established and the coastal zone of Somalia was also occupied. The need for Sister nurses for the hospital of Assab led the Minister of Foreign Affairs to begin negotiations with the Servant of God in 1885. The negotiations lasted more than a year and in November 1886 the Daughters of Saint Anne began their service in the hospital of Assab, soon extending their activity into the interior for the benefit of the native population14.

p. 13

b) Three great Popes in the era of the Servant of God.

10. — The life of the Servant of God unfolded under three Popes. In the same year Rosa Gattorno was born, Gregory XVI was elected to the pontificate. He had been Prefect of the Congregation of Propaganda Fide and had a fairly broad view of the problems of the Church in the various parts of the world.

Seen from a distance in time, the pontificate of Gregory XVI appears to us today fruitful in happy initiatives from the religious point of view, and various measures of this pope, whom the historians of the Risorgimento wished to present as the prototype of the reactionary pope, show him rather as a man of the future than a man of the past. The inhabitants of the Papal States, concerned more with their immediate interests than with the progress of the universal Church, reproached their sovereign, the pontiff, and the Secretary of State, Cardinal Lambruschini, for their reluctance to reorganize the Papal States on more modern foundations. The desire for reforms and the national aspirations during the last years of the pontificate of Gregory XVI had developed to such a point that the populations «everywhere chafed at the bit and were impatient to break it»15.

11. — In 1846 Pius IX was elected Pope. He found a social environment overheated by political tensions, alive everywhere, in search of forms of government that would allow greater participation by all classes of citizens. The amnesty for political offenses made him well regarded by all; the granting of the constitution in 1848 aroused general enthusiasm. But the action of Mazzinian infiltrators, or of other political hues, succeeded in changing the situation within the capital and in the main cities. The subsequent assassination of the prime minister Pellegrino Rossi dealt the final blow to the hopes of collaboration between the pontiff and the new social and political forces that demanded more room in the civil administration of the State.

Mazzinians and Jacobins gained the upper hand and the Pope decided to flee so as not to find himself a prisoner of a situation slipping from his hands. At Gaeta, where he had taken refuge, his position of closure toward liberalism and the unionist movement matured, while he felt the need to turn to Austria and France to restore order in the Papal States. Returning to Rome in 1850, he committed himself fully to improving the administration of the State and promoting industry, commerce, railways and new roads.

The Servant of God was bound to this Pope by deep love and veneration. She had met him for the first time on 3 January 1866 and the Pontiff commanded her to carry out the foundation, prophesying its rapid expansion. From 1866 to 1878 the relationship with the Pope was quite close, the meetings frequent; Pius IX treated the Servant of God with great affability and wanted her Sisters for the people's school he had established in the area called the Parrocchietta in Rome, and gave the Servant of God money to buy the small property16. During the pontificate of Pius IX the unity of Italy was accomplished, which marked the end of the temporal power of the Pope.

12. — Leo XIII was known to the Servant of God when he was still Archbishop of Perugia, she having opened a school in his diocese in 1875. She then met him, received in papal audience, a few more times: in 1885; in November 1886, on which occasion she presented to him the missionaries about to leave for Africa; and in October 1888 with the 180 superiors who had taken part in the General Chapter, presided over by Cardinal Alimonda.

During his pontificate Pope Leo XIII sought significant rapprochements with the Italian government with a view to a conciliation, at least to ease the friction. He maintained, however, his attitude of closure regarding the participation of Catholics in the political life of the country. He succeeded in placing the Church in a better dialogue with modern society; he gave impetus to the formation of the working masses and to the organization of the laity active in the various social realities. He promoted a better and sound philosophical and theological formation of the clergy, calling them back to sound Thomism. He was a promoter of pontifical academies of theology and of Christian archaeology, which in that period reached the peak of its success. He opened the Vatican Secret Archive to scholars for a more serious and objective approach to Church History. He continued the work of his predecessor in promoting devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus and devotion to Our Lady, especially by dedicating a month to her with the recitation of the rosary17.

p. 15

c) Women's institutes in the era of the Servant of God.

13. — The suppression of the religious Corporations carried out by Napoleon I put the vitality of women's institutes to a very harsh test. But, with the fall of the emperor, during the Restoration, there was a rapid recovery of the women's institutes already in existence. At the same time there was a flowering of new foundations of women religious, no longer solely of contemplative life but with ever stronger commitments to serve man in his perennial needs, made more acute by the social change under way in the nation. During the nineteenth century 198 institutes of pontifical right arose in Italy, to which must be added other institutes of diocesan right that had a short life. Most of the new foundations arose in northern Italy, like that of Mother Rosa Gattorno, but a good number also came to life in central and southern Italy. In 1881 Italian women religious were estimated at about 40,000.

These religious women, keeping their gaze fixed on Jesus, who drew near to man as physician, as good Samaritan, as patient teacher, as one in solidarity who takes our infirmities upon himself, turned to the most urgent needs of country people, of workers, of those who emigrated to the cities because of growing industrialization, but especially of children, through schools, hospitals, orphanages, homes for the chronically ill, rehabilitation houses for prostitutes who wished to leave that life, welcome houses for adolescent girls and young women workers living far from their home towns, workhouses to start adolescent girls on learning a trade and especially what was needed to support a family economy.

The wave of new foundations was certainly a push from the Spirit of God, who animates the Church and makes her attentive to the needs of people in every age. Yet the multiplication of institutes with the same purpose was also influenced by the fragmentation of Italy before unity and by the situation of the dioceses which, because of Napoleonic legislation first and the Italian government afterward, found themselves without religious Confraternities that had taken care of many works of social assistance. Each diocese liked to have the security of a group of women religious for its pastoral work, which could be carried out only with the contribution of these consecrated women as well.

The congregations, therefore, were generally small, and this not infrequently had a negative effect on formation and increased the disproportion between the work and the real strength of the Sisters. They generally submitted to a very demanding schedule because the requests for help from the bishops and the people were many; moreover, the congregations were very poor, and so the Sisters could carry out their social works only at the cost of great sacrifices.

The flowering of foundations and the expansion of women's religious life in Italy offered women a new space in society and in the Church. The consecrated woman made a great contribution to preserving the faith among the people, to evangelization in the new urban agglomerations and in mission lands, to which the Italian women's religious institutes gave a significant contribution. The Servant of God herself was glad to send a contingent of Sisters to Africa as early as 188618.

CHAP. III
BRIEF ACCOUNT OF THE LIFE OF THE SERVANT OF GOD

a) Birth and family environment.

14. — The Servant of God was born in the city of Genoa on 14 October 1831, to Francesco Gattorno and Adelaide Campanella. On the same day she was baptized in the parish of St. Donatus and given the names Rosa Maria Benedetta19. As long as she lived in the family she was called by the diminutive Nina.

Her father was a grain merchant and assured the family a comfortable life. An austere, almost stern person, he had great moral uprightness, as Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process, attests:

«I believe that her father was rather indifferent in matters of religion; he was, however, very honest and upright, austere in the government of the family. I seem to have read in some memoir that at his death he left part of his estate to pious works»20.

Her mother, although the sister of the well-known Mazzinian Federico Campanella, who belonged to Freemasonry, in which for a time he held the office of Grand Master, was a woman of intense piety, as Sr. A. Giuseppina Tornatore, witness III at the Roman Process, remembers her:

«I knew Mrs. Adelaide personally; she was a woman of much prayer»21.

p. 17

Others attest that she was a «holy woman», sensitive to the needs of the poor22.

The Gattorno spouses had six children: Emmanuele, Rosa (our Servant of God), Giustina, Federico, Elisa and Francesco; to these must be added Amalia, whom the mother had had from her first marriage to Gerolamo Ravano; the brothers and sisters were always on excellent terms with one another and also with their half-sister as long as she lived under their roof. They received a Christian upbringing in the family, above all through their mother; the boys, however, soon withdrew from her influence. Indeed Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, witness V at the Roman Process, attests:

«She herself (the Servant of God) used to tell me that, despite her mother's concern for the Christian education of the children (and to discipline them better she had placed them in a boarding school, where Federico did not want to stay because of his liveliness), they did not turn out as their mother would have wished, and they were a constant worry to the Servant of God for their eternal salvation; she prayed much for them and invited her religious and me to pray»23.

Elisa Gattorno, sister of the Servant of God, witness I at the Genoa Rogatorial Process, confirms it thus:

«My family was exemplarily Christian and of civil condition [...]. The upbringing in the family was Christian for all, for my mother especially24 was a holy woman»25.

b) Childhood and youth.

15. — In the early childhood of the Servant of God there were no particularly notable events.

Her schooling was done at home, with private teachers, while the boys attended the public schools. Elisa Gattorno, sister of the Servant of God, witness I at the Genoa Rogatorial Process, recalls it:

«The upbringing in the family was Christian for all, for my mother especially was a holy woman, and it was at the same time such as befits a respectable family. The boys attended the public schools. For us girls, special governesses came to the house. I know all these things from direct knowledge, given my living together with the family»26.

The subjects were those suited to young women of good family, who were not to concern themselves with public life but with running a household and being able to hold their own in conversation in society. The Servant of God therefore learned Italian letters, French, drawing and music; she acquired particular skill in embroidery and singing.

From childhood she gave signs of uncommon goodness and helpfulness; in the family she was much loved and returned that love. Sr. A. Giuseppina Tornatore, witness III at the Roman Process, recalls:

«From conversations with the Servant of God and with her relatives I formed the conviction that she completed her education in the family in a Christian manner. I likewise learned that she was much loved, especially by her mother; that, when she was a little older, being the firstborn, she helped her mother in the various household chores. From relatives I learned that she was good and submissive, and from the whole I could infer that she was of a judicious temperament»27.

Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, witness V at the Roman Process, speaks of the small and great tasks that the Servant of God carried out in the family as the eldest sister:

«From childhood the Servant of God was exemplary. My fellow sisters tell me that she was always obedient to her parents; and the Servant of God herself told me that from childhood she had from her mother the keeping of the wardrobe and the pantry, and also the task of directing the kitchen and watching over her brothers and the maids, something that naturally could not have happened unless her mother had been fully pleased with her; the Servant of God also told me that her mamma loved her very much»28.

To the tasks in the family, which gradually made her take on ever greater responsibility, the Servant of God joined the spirit of piety instilled in her by her mother together with great charity toward the poor. In this regard Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process, testifies:

«The Servant of God from her earliest years showed a very lively temperament, but was always at the same time very pious. As she grew older she took care of the household chores, I think in particular the pantry and the wardrobe [...]. From a young girl she was very devoted to piety and inclined to charity. Since she kept the household pantry, she took advantage of it to help the poor little daughters of the peasants, as I heard from her herself»29.

Francesco Gattorno, brother of the Servant of God, witness II at the Genoa Rogatorial Process, recalls with affection and clarity in his deposition the self-giving and the special charity toward the sick shown by the Servant of God:

«My sister, as soon as she was old enough and before being given in marriage, was like the soul of our father's house. I remember, both from having observed it and from having heard it from Mamma, that with an activity and self-denial worthy of every praise she carried out for the most part the domestic duties, devoting to them all the time left over from that in which she attended to her own instruction.

My mother suffered from frequent attacks of suffocation; the sister immediately younger than Rosa was frail, also as a result of a surgical operation in which she was assisted by Rosa; the other sister was still very small. In addition there was in the house our maternal grandmother, in need of continual care because of her age; and we were also at home, two brothers younger than she and the eldest, and so she had to bear continuous and heavy work. This she sustained without any complaint, with admirable diligence, so that everything in the house went in order, nothing was lacking to anyone and, especially with our old grandmother and then ill until death, with Mamma in her sufferings, with the frailer sister and with all of us she lavished the most loving care. So that her departure from the family was a grave loss for it.

She distinguished herself by her spirit of charity; she loved to make directly herself certain distributions to the poor customary in the family; everything she could dispose of she gave to the needy, and especially at the Bocchetta of St. Francis of Albaro, where the family went to the country, she was sought out by all for her charity. Even afterward, and for many years, they asked me, gratefully, for news of her»30.

16. — We do not know on what date the Servant of God made her first Communion, nor have particular memories of that event come down to us; she assimilated it as the driving center of Christian life, as the singular Eucharistic piety she developed and lived until the end of her life clearly shows. We do know, on the other hand, the day of her Confirmation, received on 19 April 1843; it was administered to her in the parish of Our Lady of the Vineyards by Cardinal Placido Tadini, Archbishop of Genoa.

These Sacraments undoubtedly marked a notable progress and a notable maturing in the Christian life of the Servant of God, since, having reached the threshold of youth, she was so rooted in faith and charity that she aroused the admiration of Mazzinians and Freemasons who, out of friendship with her uncle Federico Campanella, assiduously frequented her house. Her brother Francesco, witness II at the Genoa Rogatorial Process, recalls it, he too with admiration:

«Though not seeking glory, she won the esteem of all, even of the opponents of her religious and political ideas.

I must recall that in the family there was Federico Campanella, brother of my mother, who was a republican, an intimate follower of Giuseppe Mazzini. He had also been a fellow student of Msgr. Salvatore Magnasco, later Archbishop of Genoa, with whom, fairly frequently, as students, they used to visit Goffredo Mameli and his family at Fontanegli, in the Val Bisagno. My brother Federico too was serving among the Garibaldians and the Mazzinians and was a colonel on the general staff of Giuseppe Garibaldi. For this reason my sister Rosa happened to meet several times people of the party opposed to hers, who came to our house. She never yielded in matters of ideas, but by the sincerity of her faith, the delicacy of her manner and the goodness she showed in everything, she won from them too unlimited esteem»31.

c) Marriage and family life.

17. — Having reached the age of youth, the Servant of God had to look to her future and discuss it seriously with the one who directed her in the spirit. The biographer notes:

«She had had the good fortune to meet very worthy priests throughout her spiritual life: but at the moment of choosing a state, God had put in her path a holy minister of his, the priest Antonio Accinelli, who, having come to know her soul thoroughly and knowing her sincere in seeking the divine will, brought her to decide for marriage. He did not, in fact, see in the holy young woman the clear signs of a virginal vocation [...] all the more so since she, while cherishing in her heart a state wholly consecrated to God, felt herself also disposed to conjugal life, provided it was holily constituted. To this was added the express wish of her parents, which in those circumstances Rosa took as a sign of the divine will»32.

Among those who frequented the Gattorno house and were left admiring the grace, maturity and attractiveness of the Servant of God were her third cousin Gerolamo Custo and the lawyer Tito Orsini: both had asked for her hand. Gerolamo felt closer to Rosa, who returned his feeling with an uncommon affection, but her father had admitted Orsini's request. Shortly afterward, Francesco Gattorno had to reconsider the trust he had placed in the lawyer Orsini and no longer admitted him to the house. Gerolamo Custo then renewed his request, which was accepted. The vicissitudes of the marriage are recalled by Elisa Gattorno, sister of the Servant of God, witness I at the Genoa Rogatorial Process, in her deposition:

«On her parents' advice she decided to marry at about nineteen [...]. She had been asked for by the famous lawyer Orsini and by a cousin of ours, Gerolamo Custo. She would have preferred the cousin; nevertheless, to comply with Papa's wish, she had agreed to marry Orsini. The latter then, by his conduct and with trifling pretexts, prolonging the conclusion of the marriage negotiations, displeased Papa, who no longer admitted him to the house. When this was known, our cousin Custo renewed his request, and the marriage was concluded, the due dispensations having been obtained on account of the kinship»33.

According to many testimonies34, the Servant of God would have wished to consecrate her virginity to the Lord and was induced to marry solely out of obedience to her parents. Sr. A. Maddalena Terzaghi, witness III at the Neapolitan Rogatorial Process, expresses it thus:

«In general, from some persons in Genoa whom I cannot specify and who were in intimate relation with the Servant of God and her family, as well as from some Genoese sisters, I learned that the Servant of God desired to consecrate her virginity to the Lord, and that then, in order to obey her parents, sure of thereby doing the will of God, she agreed to go on to marriage. She prepared for marriage with prayers, vigils, fasts and austerities, as the persons mentioned above told me»35.

Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni, witness I at the Piacenza Rogatorial Process, also affirms:

«Solely to obey her own parents and follow the advice of her confessor, she chose the married state. In the will of her parents and the advice of her confessor she clearly saw in this the will of the Lord»36.

18. — The marriage was celebrated on 5 November 1852 at home, according to the custom of distinguished families at that time, and the following day the couple received the solemn blessing and heard Mass in the sacristy chapel of the cathedral of Genoa37.

A promising future of happiness thus opened for the Servant of God. But the Lord wished to lead his servant along the way of sacrifice and the cross: the succession of ever more painful events brought the Servant of God to a total stripping of herself and of her own plans, and disposed her to welcome generously the plan God had for her.

The brother of the Servant of God, Francesco Gattorno, witness II at the Genoa Rogatorial Process, effectively describes the first period of the marriage:

«The marriage was an outright disaster and a cause to my sister of continual sorrows and sacrifices. The hoped-for happiness went away with the carriage of the wedding journey. We accompanied her for a stretch, that is, as far as Varazze, on the nuptial journey; then, we relatives having returned home, she continued to Nice and Marseilles, where her husband's financial failure awaited her. She immediately appealed to Papa, who rushed to Marseilles to bring, in that desperate case, such help as was still possible, thus managing to save some small thing from that financial shipwreck, and then had to bring his daughter back to Genoa with her husband, taking them into the paternal home»38.

Amid these painful events the Servant of God had begun her motherhood, and it is easy to imagine the sinister repercussions that must have come to her health precisely in those months so much in need of peace. On 8 December 1853, the feast of the Immaculate Conception, she gave birth to a baby girl who was immediately baptized in the metropolitan church of St. Lawrence with the name Carlotta. But this time too the happiness was short-lived: a few months later a violent illness left little Carlotta deaf-mute.

Two years later, on 28 October 1855, in the family villa at Sampierdarena, her second child was born: Alessandro, who was baptized the next day in the parish of St. Martin and St. Mary della Cella.

Her husband Gerolamo, meanwhile, had managed to put his affairs on a better footing and the little family again had a home of its own and settled in the territory of the parish of St. Syrus. Shortly afterward Gerolamo Custo, who had joined in business with his brother-in-law Federico, left with him for Russia hoping to consolidate his position: Federico, in fact, had opened a trading house at Berdyansk on the Sea of Azov. He succeeded, but at the cost of his health; he returned definitively from Russia in 1857 because he was ill with pulmonary tuberculosis. At first his condition seemed to improve, but it was a brief illusion: they had barely time to rejoice at the birth of their third child, Francesco, in December of that year 1857, and to present him at the baptismal font on the 15th of the same month, when Gerolamo's health declined rapidly.

19. — The Servant of God, though absorbed in caring for the newborn and the other two little ones, would not yield to anyone the place beside her sick husband and gave him continual assistance day and night, without even undressing. Gerolamo Custo died on 9 March 1858, at the age of 31.

Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, witness V at the Roman Process, who was in intimate relation with the Servant of God and gathered some fleeting confidences of hers about these events, testifies:

«Her husband died after enduring an illness of three months during which the Servant of God never left him, neither day nor night. I remember that the Servant of God told me that her husband, even when he felt ill, did not want to omit saying the rosary every evening, and they spoke together of spiritual things, as in fact had also been done in previous years when her husband was in health. Such a loss cost the heart of the Servant of God much and, as soon as the death was ascertained, she fell into a faint; yet her soul was always resigned to the will of God, as she herself told me. She had very many Masses offered for the soul of her husband and every year, on the anniversary of his death, she had others celebrated»39.

This precious testimony shows us that the family of the Servant of God was exemplarily Christian, for it was not only united by great love but was also founded on common prayer and spiritual dialogue: it was, in other words, a true «domestic church».

Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process, affirms that «the Servant of God loved her husband very much and was always submissive to him»40.

Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, witness V at the Roman Process, also speaks of this love and of the family concord:

«The Servant of God told me that her husband was very good and that it would have been a sin to wrong him in any way, and therefore they lived together in peace and love»41.

Sr. A. Maddalena Terzaghi, witness III at the Neapolitan Rogatorial Process, adds: «The married life of the Servant of God was full of piety and charity, as is reputed among those persons who approached her, and to the religious spirit by which she always felt inspired she joined the duties of a good mother toward her children»42.

Her sister Elisa Gattorno, witness I at the Genoa Rogatorial Process, further attests that the love of the Servant of God for her husband was founded on supernatural motives:

«She loved her husband in a Christian way and was in full accord with him, preserving — as far as I can know — honesty in marriage and taking great care of the house. She had three children: Carlotta, who became, when very little, deaf-mute, Alessandro and Francesco, who died after six or seven months of life»43.

d) Widowhood and first steps toward the foundation.

20. — The Servant of God at the age of 26 found herself a widow with three small children to provide for. It was a most painful trial, though faced with Christian fortitude and resignation. Cardinal Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process, attests:

p. 24

«The husband of the Servant of God died and on this so mournful occasion she spared nothing for him, both from the religious point of view and from the temporal point of view: I know that he received the Sacraments of the Church and died as a good Christian. This trial was borne by the Servant of God with sorrow, but together with signs of resignation»44.

In her suffering the Servant of God sought refuge and comfort in faith. From the account she herself left us, we know that after her husband's death she felt the need to bring the little orphans before the altar of Our Lady of Sorrows, to entrust them to the Virgin's maternal protection45.

But the sorrow was to reach an even more dramatic point: barely three months after her husband's death, the Servant of God saw her youngest little son die as well. Francesco was the only one born in that house which could be called hers; he was the last flower of her motherhood, the last and liveliest memory of her departed husband. The trial seemed to exceed her strength, so much so that her confessor, Fr. Firpo, thought it necessary to go to her every day to comfort her. Concerning these events Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process, has left us this deposition:

«The Servant of God used to tell us sisters that she suffered very, very much at the death of her husband [...]. ‘Whereas, however — the Servant of God said with a sentiment of humility — I easily resigned myself to the loss of my husband, though with sorrow, I could not find a way to resign myself to the loss of my last child, which occurred very shortly after that of my husband. And the sorrow was so strong that to comfort me my confessor, Fr. Firpo, thought it necessary to come often to comfort me at my house every day. I felt I was going mad with grief; I no longer combed my hair and almost neglected the other two little ones’»46.

p. 25

She felt the sorrow of her husband's death extraordinarily; she returned to her father's house because her father-in-law Custo did not wish to take care of the family left widowed, preferring other brothers, and so our family took on the commitment to place the little orphans suitably»47.

21. — Under the wise guidance of her confessor, Fr. Giuseppe Firpo, the Servant of God «gave herself to a life of greater Christian perfection», as Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni, witness I at the Piacenza Rogatorial Process, affirms48. Immediately after her husband's death she made a vow of chastity and of obedience for one year, and the following year she was able to make them perpetual. She enrolled in the Third Order of St. Francis and felt an intense desire to afflict the body with bodily austerities: already during her marriage she had made a vow of perpetual fasting. She tied a small crucifix tightly to her breast, which sank into the flesh: she kept it for 5 years, then out of obedience had to remove it. It was 1864. She assiduously cultivated the sacramental life, as her confessor attests49, and prayer: she received the Eucharist every day, something uncommon at that time; she spent long hours in prayer, during which God favored her with high mystical gifts. Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, witness XX at the Roman Process, testifies in this regard:

«The Servant of God told me that her most beautiful hours in those times were those of the night: after putting her children to bed, she stayed until midnight and even until one o'clock in prayer, the hours passing quickly for her at the feet of her Crucifix»50.

So much fervor and so much love could not remain enclosed within her person. In Genoa Catholic volunteer work had a long tradition and the Servant of God took part in it naturally, as a spontaneous need to expand that love for Christ which she felt growing every day within her. She assiduously frequented the Pammatone Hospital and assisted other sick people at home, always preferring the poorest or those shunned by all. She joined numerous associations that flourished in Genoa, among them the Pious Unions for Eucharistic adoration, the Pious Association for the preservation and increase of the Catholic faith, founded by the Servant of God Fr. Giuseppe Frassinetti, and above all the Pious Union of the Daughters of Mary Immaculate, founded at Mornese by Angela Maccagno and promoted in Genoa by Frassinetti himself. Soon the Servant of God, through her availability and zeal, became the soul of the associations to which she belonged and a point of reference for other committed people.

22. — This fervor and this manifold commitment are recalled in his deposition by Francesco Gattorno, brother of the Servant of God, witness II at the Genoa Rogatorial Process:

«After her husband's death Rosa devoted herself to extraordinary works of piety and charity, especially going to the Pammatone hospital. At first she was guided by her own judgment, then she entered into relation with Msgr. Charvaz, Archbishop of Genoa, and with Fr. Firpo, her confessor, who guided her in her works of piety and beneficence. Several times I saw the priest Firpo come to our house for this purpose»51.

The work of the Servant of God toward her children and parents during the period of widowhood is well brought out by the biographer:

«Her many penances and assiduous prayers did not keep her from thinking of others: indeed, the industriousness of the pious widow aroused much wonder in Genoa, present in very many charitable institutions and always ready for charitable requests. Before all else, however, she devoted herself to her children, whom she loved tenderly. Mindful that one cannot please God who does not care for his own, and above all for those of his household, she turned with all her soul ablaze with faith to those tender creatures of hers, to educate them as well as she could and make their childhood full and happy: so that she saw with sweet surprise the generous piety of her own heart soon transfused into those two hearts.

Carlotta, the deaf-mute, grew innocent and candid; but because of that infirmity she could not so easily profit from her mother's teachings. Therefore, to prevent her from remaining backward or in any case unfit to live according to her social rank, it was decided to place her in the Royal Institute for the Deaf-Mute in Milan, directed at that time by the zealous and pious priest Eliseo Ghislandi.

Rosa accompanied her there at the beginning of 1864 and stayed in Milan several weeks to accustom her little daughter gradually to the new way of life. She succeeded so well that she left her very happy in the Institute, where by her artless innocence, gentle manners and inclination to piety she won everyone's sympathy.

Alessandro, on the other hand, called at that time by his relatives by the pet name Giggio, remained at home for some time; he showed from his earliest years an open intelligence and a very lively and affectionate character; hence very soon he drew from his mamma generous sentiments of piety. Barely nine years old, he often repeated that he wanted to become a priest: so in the autumn of 1864, to preserve him from the contagion of bad companions, it was thought to entrust him to a private school; that of preparation for ecclesiastical studies at Carignano was chosen52.

p. 27

Four years later the boy entered the ecclesiastical college, or seminary, at Savona, directed by the Priests of the Mission [...].

To these cares for her children and to the charitable assistance of the poor and sick, Rosa added the most affectionate attentions for her parents, and especially for her mother, always frail in health: this spending of herself on behalf of all, while she was seen to decline in strength each day, made all the more admirable the smile of goodness she spread around her, suggesting a hidden strength of spirit, certainly different from that which arises from ordinary natural affection»53.

23. — In 1863 or at the beginning of 1864, the Servant of God Fr. Giuseppe Frassinetti found himself needing to provide for the appointment of a new president of the Pious Union of the Daughters of Mary Immaculate in Genoa and had thought at once of Rosa Gattorno, but, knowing her humility and fearing that she would refuse a task that put her in the public eye, he turned to her spiritual director, Fr. Firpo, to induce her to accept. Moreover, Frassinetti had realized that the spirit of the Pious Union corresponded fully to the Company of St. Ursula founded by St. Angela Merici: he had therefore reworked the rule, entitling it Rule of the Pious Union of the New Ursulines, Daughters of St. Mary Immaculate, under the Protection of St. Ursula and St. Angela Merici, and had presented it to the Archbishop of Genoa for approval, receiving a negative reply. Frassinetti, turning to the Servant of God, whom he knew to be held in high esteem by Msgr. Charvaz, made her a twofold request: to accept the presidency of the Pious Union and to obtain approval of the rule. The Servant of God reserved the right to hear the archbishop's opinion. He, receiving her in audience, ordered her to guess what he disapproved of in the rule. The Servant of God was somewhat surprised, but obeyed. She herself tells in the Memoirs54 that that evening during prayer she asked for and obtained particular lights to correct the rule, according to the archbishop's will; having done this she resumed praying and thanking her Crucifix and was once again rapt in ecstasy. During this second rapture she heard the voice of her Beloved as if dictating to her a new rule, for a different work, and commanded her to write it.

Returning to Msgr. Charvaz she brought him the corrections; the archbishop was satisfied and approved Frassinetti's rule, but the Servant of God made no mention to him of the new rule that had been inspired in her.

Some time later the Servant of God began to feel tormented by the thought of the new foundation, which would oblige her to leave her children. This struggle is recalled by Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process, who lived in intimate familiarity with the Servant of God:

«On that night in which the Servant of God, as I said, was praying before her Crucifix that it might give her light about Frassinetti's manual, she told me that she felt an interior movement by which she understood that she would have to found an Institute. And I think she added that the Lord's inspiration was so vehement that it obliged her to put down on paper at once some notes for such a foundation. These notes, however, she wrote as if beside herself, and when she had come completely to herself and read her notes with a cool mind, she was assailed by the thought of her children and had such torment that, no longer able to bear the sight of that writing, she put it away in a cupboard without looking at it for some time. The voice of God, however, gave her no peace inwardly, and she then resolved to speak of it to her confessor, Fr. Firpo; and I think Fr. Firpo reproached her for not having told him at once, and advised her to go to the archbishop to speak to him about it. If I remember rightly, she did not have the courage to go to the archbishop in person and preferred to write to him. The archbishop then sent for her and, when he had heard from the Servant of God the details of what she had hinted at in the letter, he told her flatly that it was the will of God and that she must set to work»55.

24. — Before deciding to turn to the Pope, the Servant of God turned to other persons who by their holiness or wisdom could help her discern the will of God. At that time the Capuchin lay brother St. Francis of Camporosso was carrying on a vast apostolate of charity in Genoa; the Servant of God met him several times because of the works that united them on behalf of the poor. To him the Servant of God turned in her doubts. We read, in fact, in the deposition of Sr. A. Giuseppina Tornatore, witness II at the Roman Process:

«I remember hearing from the Servant of God that on one occasion among others, having gone to the Ven. Francis of Camporosso, who was then in Genoa, he showed himself trembling for the grave tribulations to which she would be subjected in the future and which he saw in spirit. I think he predicted something to her, adding: ‘Take courage, my daughter, I will pray for you’. This happened when the Servant of God was pondering in her heart the foundation of the Institute»56.

Around 1864 the Servant of God had met in Genoa the priest Fr. Luigi Cogrossi, who was surrounded by a reputation as a healer and saint. With the archbishop's permission she began to confess to him and progressively left the direction of Fr. Firpo, who had guided her until that moment. Cogrossi encouraged her in the foundation and offered his help: he had, in fact, many acquaintances in various dioceses of Italy and in Rome.

p. 29

The Servant of God, in the difficult choice between the foundation of the Institute and her duties as a mother, wished to submit to the supreme decision of the Pontiff, sure that in this way she would fulfill the will of God. Accompanied by her friend Teresa Porta, widow Morasso, and provided with letters of recommendation, she arrived in Rome in January 1866. On the 3rd she had the papal audience. She was certain that the Pope would take into account that she was a mother of a family and therefore would not lay on her the heavy burden of the foundation; the Lord, however, was about to let her experience how far his thoughts surpass human thoughts. Even after many years she recalled precisely in her Memoirs the dialogue that took place with Pius IX:

«[...] As soon as I was at his holy feet, Pius IX blessed me and, raising me with the hand that held mine, told me that he had read those rules and that they were truly beautiful and that I must not delay putting them into effect. Oh! I threw myself on the ground and, weeping, said to him: ‘Holy Father, I have two children, an elderly father and mother, and both my children are small!’. He answered me: ‘It does not matter, God wills it so’. ‘Oh! no, Holy Father! God, according to the holy Gospel, will ask me to account for my children — and I was weeping uncontrollably — I love them too much, I cannot leave them. Holy Father, it is impossible!’.

The Holy Father stops and in a severe tone says to me: ‘Very well: if you do not do what God wants of you, you will have remorse, for the whole time of your life your conscience will gnaw at you and you will have no more peace’. I was frightened and: ‘No, Holy Father — I answered him — I want to do the will of God’. He resumed: ‘Good’; in a manner as if inspired he said to me: ‘This Institute will spread rapidly, like the flight of the dove, to all parts of the world. God will take care of your children: you take care of God in his work’»57.

The Servant of God, shattered, spent the whole night weeping and the next day went to the church of St. Marcellus on the Corso and prayed before the altar of Our Lady of Sorrows. During the prayer she remained absorbed, her tears dried, and in the Virgin she gained peace and strength. Restored, she found herself transformed, and offered herself as a victim for the Work of the Lord58.

e) The foundation.

25. — After the Pope's audience, the Servant of God stayed in Rome several days, during which Fr. Luigi Cogrossi introduced her to various ecclesiastical personalities. On the return journey to Genoa, Cogrossi also proposed that she stop in Piacenza to meet two priests of excellent spirit: the canons Chiappini; they took great interest in the foundation and begged her to begin the work in Piacenza, a quiet city led by an excellent bishop, and offered to look for a rented apartment as a first residence: later a suitable palace could easily be bought, since many were for sale.

p. 30

A short time later the Servant of God received word from the priests Chiappini that they had found the apartment; she therefore had to decide quickly and informed the archbishop. Msgr. Charvaz, who hoped much from the new Institute in his diocese, objected to its beginning elsewhere. The Servant of God was aware of having acted solely under the guidance of God's will: she therefore had recourse to prayer and, returning to the archbishop, found him changed; he gave her his blessing, but did not accept her resignation from the various associations and asked her to return periodically to look after them.

The last obstacle to overcome was the opposition of her parents, who absolutely did not want to let her leave, above all her mother. In this regard Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process, testifies:

«The Servant of God, having obtained the archbishop's consent, secretly, with the help of some person, sent much of her belongings and furniture to Piacenza, to the house which, as I said, the canons Chiappini had offered her [...]. Having done this she laid her plan before the family, and naturally all hell broke loose. Her good mamma was especially upset, because she was elderly and sickly and saw herself assisted by her daughter with so much love and sacrifice, even at the cost of entire nights of rest. The Servant of God nevertheless showed herself always calm and fearless. The Servant of God had already gathered for her foundation some young Genoese women, and when the moment of departure came, her good mother, to dissuade her from abandoning her, lay stretched out on the threshold of the door saying: ‘Let us see if you have the courage to walk over my body’. The Servant of God then (it is always she who told me these things) took a leap and flew to the station, where she found the young women she had summoned for her foundation, and left with them for Piacenza»59.

26. — The Servant of God, with her five companions, arrived in Piacenza on [...]60 she adapted the Dal Verme palace, on the Stradone Farnese; she signed the purchase contract on 25 March 1866; everything prepared, she moved there the following May.

Soon the news of the new foundation spread through the city of Piacenza and the province and many young women asked to join the community, while three of the first companions returned to their homes.

Shortly after her arrival in Piacenza, the Servant of God had met Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, of the Priests of the Mission, professor at the Alberoni College, and had chosen him as her spiritual director. As numerous letters testify, Tornatore sought to instill in the Servant of God and her companions devotion to Saint Anne and proposed that they change the name of the Institute, Daughters of Mary Immaculate, Minims of St. Francis of Assisi, to Daughters of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate.

Concerning the change of the Institute's name, Sr. A. Santina Solenghi, witness VIII at the Roman Process61, testifies:

«When the Servant of God went to Piacenza, she wanted to found the Institute of the Daughters of the Immaculate, and for this reason when I entered I found a draft of rules for the Daughters of the Immaculate, and on the high altar of the chapel there was the image of the Immaculate, while that of Saint Anne stood on a side altar. When I entered, however, the change of name to Daughters of Saint Anne had already taken place, and I believe it came about through the influence of Tornatore, of the Gentlemen of the Mission, whose direction for her Institute the Servant of God went to ask in the early times when she was in Piacenza, and Fr. Tornatore was most devoted to Saint Anne»62.

27. — The Servant of God decided that the clothing of the first five novices would take place on 8 December 1866. She asked the bishop for a priest for the preparatory spiritual exercises and he assigned Fr. Tornatore. On the day of the Immaculate Conception the clothing was performed by the vicar general, Msgr. Angelo Testa.

The Servant of God did not take the religious habit together with the first five. In this regard Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process, recalls:

«The Servant of God did not put on the religious habit with the first five, but on the feast of Saint Anne in 1867. From the Servant of God I did not learn the reason for this delay, but perhaps it was to be freer in her business affairs, because I know that she worked with the mayor and with the prefect to obtain their approval»63.

The Servant of God put on the religious habit on 26 July 1867, the feast of

p. 32

Saint Anne, together with 20 other novices64. It had been established that the novitiate would last three years. The foundress too completed the novitiate and on 8 April 1870, the feast of Our Lady of Sorrows, made her Religious Profession together with 12 other sisters65.

In August 1867 the Servant of God found herself needing to dismiss Fr. Luigi Cogrossi, who had helped her in the foundation; with humility she acknowledged having been mistaken about him66; from then on she turned more and more for counsel and help to Fr. Tornatore, who followed the Institute and also procured for it much economic aid.

From the first months of the foundation many young women asked to be admitted to the new Institute: this laid the premises for rapid expansion. In January 1867 the Servant of God was asked for nurses for the hospital of Cento.
