In the same year, when the cholera epidemic ended in Piacenza, during which the sisters had cared for the cholera victims, she took into the mother house the little girls left orphaned.

In October 1868 the Servant of God received the request of the priest Richini of Sampierdarena, who made available a small capital for a house for girls at risk and for a school.

In 1870 she opened in Piacenza a free school for boys in premises made available by the Municipality.

In 1871 she was able to open a community of home-visiting nurses in her native city, Genoa, and at the end of the same year a community in Ferrara at the invitation of Countess Trotti. In 1872 she accepted the care of the hospital of Nizza Monferrato. In 1873 she opened a community in Foligno and three in Rome.

f) The affair of the rules.

28. — The iter followed by the rules for approval was rather troubled and caused the Servant of God numerous worries and sufferings.

The Servant of God had had the overall intuition of the institute, but did not feel equally inspired to draw up a complete regulation; what was inspired in her instead was to whom she should turn: to Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore. The Servant of God speaks of this supernatural intervention in a confidential letter sent to the Holy Father Pius IX in June 1871:

«The rules that I presented to Your Holiness I did not make myself; but while I was in the chapel praying, Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, appeared to me, and the Servant of God Fr. Bernardo Maria Clausi told me to go to Mr. Tornatore, Missionary, that he would give me the book of our constitutions; three times I resisted obeying this command but the third time I was threatened and then I obeyed»67.

In February 1868 the rule was already ready and was praised by the Bishop of Piacenza, who had had it examined by a commission of theologians. It was sent at once also to the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, but received no reply. The Servant of God presented it a second time in May 1871.

The little book was examined by the consultors and then passed to the Holy Office which in January 1872 gave the order that all copies be withdrawn, without however making known to the foundress the reasons for such a decision. The measure also included the removal of the Author from the Institute. The Servant of God gave proof of submission to the Church and of heroic obedience, as can be seen from the letter addressed to the secretary of the Cardinal Protector:

«May the will of God be done upon our heads, and I, a miserable creature, with my head to the ground, adore all his dispositions and submit myself to the wishes of the Church»68.

The Servant of God was ordered to draw up a regulation herself with the help of Msgr. Giordani, auxiliary bishop of Ferrara, drawing it from observance, and this «draft of constitutions» was entrusted to Fr. Leonardo Fava, S. J., for a reworking. The Servant of God had much to suffer because there was an attempt to compose the rule of her Institute from passages of the constitutions of other similar Institutes; she therefore set out with humility, submission, but also with firmness, her reservations to the Secretary of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars on 26 March 1873:

«Two days ago I spoke with the Rev. Fr. Fava, who told me that he has not yet done anything concerning the rules and that they must be redone and it will take another five or six months; these words were so many stabs to me: two months that I am in Rome and he did nothing. My Monsignor, ah, may you grant my entreaties by joining to Fr. Fava two other Servants of God, and may they have the charity to listen to me, because if this father R. gives a new spirit to the rules, it will no longer be our spirit, he would renew another Institute. If the Church imposes on me to observe them, I, most obedient, will bow my head and try to study this new spirit. In all confidence I reveal to you a strong temptation of mine, and it is to lay everything down, not being able to bear so prolonged an agony»69.

p. 34

29. — There was also an attempt to change the name of the Institute and the Servant of God had to struggle not a little, but the intervention of the Holy Father Pius IX put an end to every discussion. Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process, recalls it in her deposition:

«The foundation began under the title of Daughters of the Immaculate. The reasons for this title and for its change to Daughters of Saint Anne I do not know well enough to say anything [...]. I know with certainty, however, that the Servant of God met with opposition to the change of name from the Protector of the Sisters of Saint Anne, Cardinal Caterini. One day, however, the Servant of God being received in audience with her sisters by the Holy Father Pius IX, he, on seeing her, exclaimed: ‘Oh! here are the Daughters of Saint Anne’. With this the discussions ended, the opposition ceased and the title of Daughters of Saint Anne remained with us. So I heard from Mr. Tornatore»70.

In 1875 the Cardinal Protector of the Institute, Giuseppe Berardi, asked Fr. Tornatore to compile a rule again himself, since no one could manage it. The Father, by now reinstated in the Institute after so many insistences by the Servant of God, set to work and this rule was presented at the beginning of 1876 to the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars and shortly afterward, in April, the Institute received the decree of praise and three years later the decree of definitive approval71. The definitive approval of the Constitutions, on the other hand, was given on 26 July 1892, the feast of [Saint Anne, patron] of the Servant of God. Regarding this event, the biographer writes:

«Great, then, was the joy that flooded the soul of Mother Gattorno when she received the precious little book. She received it from the maternal authority of the Church; she presented it with words of love to her daughters; she recommended its observance with all care. But she did more than verbal recommendations: she saw life in those rules; therefore, as a true mother, she offered herself as a victim to God that that life might be full in all her daughters and never fail. One cannot read without deep emotion what she left written in her Memoirs: ‘The irons I wear, when I pray, under my knees; the food I take, lean and so poor; the irons I wear on my arms and legs and the wounds they have made me, all this I offer to you, that you may grant me that your Institute never fail in the observance of the Holy Rules until the end of the world’»72

g) Government of the Institute and its development in Italy and abroad.

30. — The Institute of the Servant of God had, from the beginning, a rapid growth. As we have already noted, very many young women asked to be admitted, attracted by the foundress's reputation for holiness and by the fearless charity shown by the sisters, both in the works begun and in the emergencies of the epidemics that from time to time afflicted the population. The Servant of God, for her part, received many requests from priests and charitable congregations who wished to make use of the Institute for the benefit of the suffering in various parts of Italy.

p. 35

The main works of the Institute were: care of the sick at home and in hospitals and taking in girls in danger of being lost. To these works the Servant of God thought it good to add, from the first years, other works according to the needs that arose in the various local situations: she therefore opened free schools for the poor, nurseries, homes for the elderly, institutes for the deaf-mute, prisons.

Only 12 years after the foundation the possibility of service in the missions presented itself. Fr. Vincenzo Rocchi conducted with the Servant of God the negotiations for sending a group of sisters to Bolivia, and in November 1878 the first group of missionaries left for those distant lands. Six years later, in 1884, a request came from Brazil, and in 1886 the Italian Government asked her for nurses for the hospital of Assab: thus the mission in Eritrea and Ethiopia opened.

The Servant of God rejoiced in these foundations, since she saw the possibility of making the faith known and extending the Kingdom of God. Sr. A. Fabiana Orsi, witness II at the Roman Process, notes:

«Her faith is manifested in the prayers that she offered and had her religious offer for the conversion of unbelievers and sinners, and in having welcomed with great pleasure the opportunity to send her religious to America and Africa for the unbelievers and non-Catholics and for the spiritual good of the Eritrean colony»73.

31. — In her capacity as foundress, the Servant of God was also Superior General of her Institute and always worked with the greatest zeal for the spiritual and temporal good of the sisters.

To visit the houses the Servant of God made very frequent journeys, however much it cost her. Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process, recalls it:

«From the beginning of the foundation of the Institute I learned from the other sisters that she visited the houses very often and was always here and there, so much so that once, when asked what her address was, she answered jokingly: ‘On the railways!’».

p. 36

Sr. A. Fabiana Orsi, witness II at the Roman Process, adds:

«The Servant of God concerned herself with solicitude for disciplinary observance and for this reason not only watched over the house where she resided but also visited the others with zeal. Sometimes she wrote not only to the superiors but also to the simple religious, as she also did with me a couple of times; exhorting, encouraging, comforting»74.

The uprightness of the Servant of God in government and her charitable treatment of the sisters, above all the sick, are brought out in the deposition of Emilia Settimo, Princess of Fitalia, witness XXXI, IV ex officio, at the Roman Process:

«Once I accompanied her on her visit to Monreale, and I noticed that she brought joy, encouragement and contentment with her; it was paradise that she brought to her sisters [...].

Needless to say how much care she took of her sick sisters. They were her passion, and sometimes she even helped them miraculously. She went personally to the infirmary and cared for them herself with charity without limits»75.

Sr. A. Geronima Mazza, witness I at the Palermo Rogatorial Process, affirms that the Servant of God held the office of superior in order to obey ecclesiastical authority:

«The first directress of the Institute from its very beginnings was Sister Rosa Gattorno, and she did not put herself in this direction, but was put there by authority, that is, by the Holy Father Pius IX; and she always held it with a spirit of obedience. She never ceased to direct the Institution. During the time that she governed the Institute she always used prudence and charity in everything that concerned her office»76.

h) Relations with the family after the foundation.

32. — Called by God to found a new religious family, the Servant of God was absorbed by the cares that such an undertaking required; this, however, did not keep her from fulfilling her duties toward her natural family.

She was bound to all by tender affection; her father and her brothers Federico and Francesco were of the greatest help to her in the manifold affairs of the Institute, both as business advisers and as occasional agents and intermediaries with the various supplier firms. But altogether singular were the affection and care she had for her children.

p. 37

She had placed Alessandro in a boarding school so that he might have a suitable education. But Alessandro did not manage to finish his secondary studies, and wanted to devote himself to commerce, as was the family tradition: he went first to America in 1876, but returned after about two years; he tried other business ventures, always without success. In 1879 he confessed to his mother a fault not committed and the consequent fatherhood of a child, to wrest from her consent to marriage, and he married Maria Tellini. Two years before his death he then revealed the truth to his mother, who, to protect the Institute, had to bring a suit to disavow paternity. Since her son did not succeed in any enterprise of his own and was by now undermined by consumption, the Servant of God wished to have him live in Piacenza and had him carry out some tasks for the Institute77.

In all the vicissitudes of her son the Servant of God showed herself concerned and solicitous not only for his temporal good but also for his eternal salvation, never ceasing to pray and offer penances for this purpose. Cardinal Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process, testifies in this regard:

«About thirty years ago one of the sons of the Servant of God died, Alessandro, who, although attached to his mother, made her suffer greatly by his private conduct, and the greatest anguish of the Servant of God was to see him far from God, while a grave illness (consumption) brought him nearer to the grave day by day. The Servant of God spared nothing for his temporal health, and at the same time she worked that he might return to God, and for this purpose too she offered herself to the Lord with temporal penances. She was heard by the Lord, because her son, sent to Naples for a climatic cure, grew worse and reached the point of death. Then he confessed, pointing out that he was glad to be able to give this consolation to his mother. When the illness gave a little respite, he went to Piacenza, where he died with the last religious comforts»78.

The Servant of God had singular care also for her daughter Carlotta. As we have recalled, she had placed her in the Royal Institute for the Deaf-Mute in Milan, directed by the excellent priest Eliseo Ghislandi, and when she left it she kept her with her in the Mother House in Piacenza, together with the orphans, entrusting her from time to time to friendly families such as that of the counts Marrazzani, until she went on to marriage79.

Cardinal Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process, testifies:

«Torn away from her family, the Servant of God never neglected her duties as a mother according to the flesh, and always concerned herself with her children, especially in what concerned their morals. One must not believe, however, that she let herself be so absorbed by these cares as to neglect, even in the slightest part, her duties toward the Institute she had founded. Having procured a good education for her daughter, so that she would not be disagreeable even in conversation, she was glad, as at a providence of the Lord, to learn that a young man of the Roman aristocracy, Count Gaspare Barbiellini Amidei, had taken an interest in her daughter and had asked for her hand. Even after the marriage the Servant of God continued to concern herself with her daughter in order to make her unhappiness less painful»80.

p. 38

Carlotta married Count Gaspare Barbiellini Amidei in April 1876, and the Servant of God provided her daughter a dowry of 80,000 lire81 and consented to her buying a house near the sisters' residence in Piacenza so as to be able to look after her better, given her disability.

33. — The marriage of her daughter was for the Servant of God a source of continual sorrows until her death. Francesco Gattorno, brother of the Servant of God, witness II at the Genoa Rogatorial Process, recalls it in his deposition:

«The couple settled in Piacenza, where Rosa was then also resident, where they bought, paying at once an installment of the price, a small house with a little garden around it [...]. My sister having thus fulfilled her duties as a mother toward her daughter, should, at least in this respect, have had no troubles; but it went quite otherwise.

The daughter, egged on and pushed by her husband, sought to gain advantages not only from her mother's family property but also from what, through the work of the sisters and through donations, was being accumulated in the Institute. My sister, as she had scrupulously given her daughter what could belong to her of the family property, so she wanted strictly preserved for the Institute what belonged to it. She thus had for many years to resist the unjustified insistence of her daughter, who seized every occasion, watched every moment to find herself alone with her mother in order to repeat her demands»82.

Of the uprightness of the Servant of God toward her family Sr. A. Giuseppina Tornatore, witness III at the Roman Process, also speaks: «Of the things of the Institute, the Servant of God gave nothing to her children. If she made some gift to her daughter, and if she paid some bill for which her son-in-law sent her daughter to ask, she did this with money that some lady gave her so that she might use it not for the needs of the Institute»83.

i) The last years of life and the Apostolic Visitation.

34. — In the first 15 years from the foundation, the Servant of God exercised the government of the Institute without the help of a constituted general council, but relying on her secretary and above all on the counsel of Fr. Tornatore, who was recognized as superior in temporalibus, on the Cardinal Protector and on the diocesan bishop. This was possible both because the size of the institute still allowed it and because the constitutions with the complete norms had not yet been approved. At the Chapter of 1881 the general council was formally constituted and the Institute was divided into Provinces.

During the Chapter of 1888, presided over by Cardinal Alimonda, the Servant of God found herself needing to remove Fr. Tornatore from the Institute because the presence of two authorities risked creating an internal division. It was a painful decision for both, but the Servant of God always acted with a view to the greater good of the Institute and with the counsel of authoritative persons. After this event, their relations remained cordial until the death of Fr. Tornatore.

35. — In 1890 the Servant of God, at the insistence of some sisters, of Princess Emilia di Fitalia and of the future Cardinal Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, wrote the history of the Institute and, to avoid making known the names of the persons, above all ecclesiastics, who at different times had greatly obstructed her, used allegorical language, so as to veil the facts from anyone who did not already know them by other means84.

The Princess of Fitalia, enthusiastic about that writing, had it printed at her own expense, after submitting it to Cardinal Guarino, Archbishop of Messina, who praised the book and dictated the title that was lacking: a title unfortunately mistaken and not corresponding to the content.

In the following years some appeals against the Servant of God reached the Holy See; the ecclesiastical Authority then ordered an Apostolic Visitation, entrusting it to Abbot Domenico Serafini. In the letter of appointment, however, as the reason for the Visitation, only a generic allusion is made to inconveniences, and the publication of the book Travagli e conforti is made explicit85.

On the occasion of the Apostolic Visitation the Servant of God, though suffering inwardly because of this tribulation, showed herself submissive and obedient to the Visitor.

Sr. A. Fabiana Orsi, witness II at the Roman Process, highlights the uprightness of the Servant of God and the freedom she wished the sisters to enjoy in speaking to the Visitor:

p. 40

«I know that an Apostolic Visitation took place in our Institute, made by Msgr. Serafini, by whom I was called. I do not know the reason for such a visitation, and I recall that at that time the Servant of God was very afflicted, I do not know, however, whether for this reason. I likewise recall that the Servant of God gave no instruction on how to behave with the Visitor (at least to me she certainly gave none), and forbade the secretaries too to give me any instruction in this regard, and I believe that such prohibition applied to all. I do not know whether any measures were taken concerning this Apostolic Visitation. I believe the Visitor remained satisfied, as the secretaries told me»86.

The Servant of God did not see the end of the Apostolic Visitation, which concluded in 1903, three years after her death. The measures taken against the Institute were of slight importance and the Apostolic Visitor in his report amply acknowledged the uprightness of the Servant of God in government and administration87.

j) Last illness and serene death of the Servant of God.

36. — The Servant of God was 69 years old when the Lord called her to himself. Harsh penances, the strain of continual journeys, the difficulties of the Institute and illnesses had weakened her, but had not kept her from carrying out her mission as foundress and fulfilling her task as Superior General.

On 26 July 1899 she wished to celebrate in Rome with extraordinary solemnity the feast of Saint Anne, patroness of the Institute, as thanksgiving to the Holy Mother for the countless graces received, sensing that it was the last feast she would keep on earth. Soon, in fact, the alarming signs of the illness that was to lead her to the tomb appeared.

Advised to allow herself a little rest, she wished to go to Liguria, where she intended to visit the houses of that region. She stayed there until October and had to return to Rome accompanied by the doctor and the priest because her life was feared for.

Having arrived in Rome she seemed to recover and continued tirelessly to attend to the affairs of the Institute. In November she had the consolation of seeing consecrated bishop, in the church adjoining the generalate house, her counselor and benefactor of the Institute, Msgr. Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, appointed apostolic nuncio in Brussels.

p. 41

In February 1900 she was struck by a severe influenza and never recovered from it. The condition of her heart worsened in such a way as to foreshadow the catastrophe. Dr. Montechiari, who had long been treating the patient, declared that for about 12 years she had been affected by interstitial nephritis and that for about a year she had been subject to attacks of cardiac arrhythmia, due to arteriosclerosis88.

On 18 April the Servant of God, worried that her son-in-law Barbiellini might make claims on the goods of the Institute after her death, summoned the Notary Monti, to whom she had already delivered her holographic will, and made a declaration in which she annulled the sheets signed in blank and handed over to relatives89.

The same day she received the visit of Cardinal Mariano Rampolla, Protector of the Institute, to whom she assured that no one could make claims on the Institute after her death and that there would be no difficulties for whoever would have to govern it.

Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, witness V at the Roman Process, who was the confidante and nurse of the Servant of God in the last years of her life, attests that the foundress had signs that foretold her death:

«About a couple of months before dying the Servant of God began to see the signs foretelling her death. The first sign was the sight, three or four times, of blood on the clock that she kept on the table. Every time she saw this sign it was around midnight, and every time she, who was already in bed because she was in poor health, showed that sign to me, who was assisting her»90.

37. — The Servant of God, despite her grave illnesses, worked until three days before dying, as Sr. A. Santina Solenghi, witness VIII at the Roman Process, who was Assistant General and superior of the generalate house, recalls:

«Despite all her ailments, the Servant of God concerned herself incessantly with her Institute, gave orders, received and wrote letters. Having thus reached the third of May, that morning, when she presented herself in the office where I too was with the others of the secretariat, she made on all the most painful impression by the extraordinary pallor of her face. She sat as usual on a chair at her table, concerning herself even then with the things of her Institute. After lunch she felt so ill that they had to carry her to bed»91.

On this occasion the Servant of God, unable to do it by herself, had Sr. Anna Serafina Foglia remove the iron chain she wore at her waist. The biographer writes:

«As the swelling then increased enormously, the Mother herself called her faithful Sr. Serafina Foglia, who because of her simplicity was very close to her [...]: with her help, then, she had the chain removed that she had girded at her waist forty-two years earlier without ever taking it off. Unable to loosen that device, because the joining link had been closed, Sr. A. Serafina had to take a sturdy pair of pincers and break another link: in removing the chain, shreds of flesh were torn away»92.

On Friday 4 May the Servant of God wanted the sisters around her and thanked them, saying:

«I thank you for everything you have done for me. Now everything is averted for me», showing herself relieved and content93.

That evening she wanted in her room the image of Maria Mater gratiae et Misericordiae which had belonged to the Ven. Fr. Bernardo Maria Clausi, and rose from her bed to pray for a few minutes, then asked to receive Communion as Viaticum. They wanted to dissuade her, but she insisted; so it was brought to her by Fr. Agostino Donadio. It was the last Communion she was able to make, no longer being able to swallow afterward94.

In the last days of her life the Servant of God was always absorbed in prayer, as the sisters saw from the glance she turned from time to time to her Crucifix.

On Saturday evening, her confessor Fr. Vincenzo da Alatri asked her whether she wished to receive the Anointing of the Sick; unable to speak, she signed yes and received it with great devotion; the papal blessing was also brought to her. She then entered into agony and was continually assisted by her confessor and by Fr. Agostino Donadio95.

38. — The Servant of God died amid general lamentation96. The last services to her body were rendered by Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, helped by two other sisters, and in laying her out on the bed in the very room of her death, they saw on her body various scars, unmistakable signs of the instruments of penance used for a long time97.

The body of the Servant of God remained on view in her room on Sunday and Monday and a great many people came to see her, priests, religious, persons of every class98.

The funeral of the Servant of God is recalled thus by Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process:

«The body was laid out in the room where she died until Monday morning [...]; it was placed in a triple coffin, one of them of zinc [...]. I know that many brought rosaries and other objects of piety to touch to the body, and asked for something of the Servant of God. She had a truly serene and beautiful appearance [...]. Enclosed in the coffin, she was taken to our chapel where she remained until Tuesday morning, when she was taken to our church where the funeral was held with a great concourse of people, so that the church was full. In the afternoon she was taken to Campo Verano with a great procession. Her brothers also attended, but her son-in-law Gaspare greeted the body in the church and left. The Congregation of the Daughters of Mary of here and of our school at Prati was there with their Directors [...]. The newspapers gave ample accounts, which were more or less truthful»99.

In the cemetery the body of the Servant of God was placed in the tomb of the Institute, in the quadriportico. The following year, a chapel having been built in the place called «Pincetto vecchio», she was transferred there and placed above the entrance door, facing the altar.

After 32 years, with the permission of the ecclesiastical Authority, it was desired to transfer the body of the foundress to the Institute's church on Via Merulana. On 8 February the recognition was carried out and the body, beneath the putrefied garments, was found incorrupt and flexible. On 14 June the body was transferred beneath the floor of the church adjoining the generalate house and in 1961 it was moved to a more visible niche, still within the generalate house.

In 1981 a new recognition was carried out and the body was found incorrupt. On 9 December, after the solemn Mass presided over by Cardinal Vicar Ugo Poletti, the body of the Servant of God was entombed in the church adjoining the generalate house.

p. 44

CHAP. IV
THE HEROICITY OF THE VIRTUES IN GENERAL

39. — It is most favorably striking that the witnesses, when asked to judge the whole of the virtues exercised by the Servant of God, declared without the slightest shadow of doubt that she was a person who stood out in everything; and similar statements, which we shall now see, do not come from hasty opinions, but are the fruit of reasoned and personal findings of fact, resting on quite precise grounds and confirmed by what the witnesses, in answer to the following questions, will report as proof of each of the virtues.

In the procedural depositions of the individual witnesses and in the many documents contained in the second part of this our Positio, the heroicity with which the Servant of God Mother Rosa Gattorno practiced the virtues throughout her whole life is evident, from childhood to youth, from marriage to widowhood, from the beginning of the foundation of the Institute and throughout her religious life until death. She was truly faithful to her duties and constant, without pause or weakening, in the exercise of all the Christian virtues, theological and cardinal or moral. In everything and for everything she strove always to conform her life, even in the smallest details, to the fulfillment of the sovereign will of God.

Here is how His Eminence Cardinal Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process, expresses himself on this matter:

«I do not doubt the heroism of the theological virtues of the Servant of God and of her cardinal virtues, nor of her mortification, chastity, poverty, obedience. This heroism is manifestly proved by the grave difficulties generously overcome by the Servant of God, by the extraordinary harshness of her penances, in which she evidently manifested the desire to be wholly a victim of her God, as it might please Him. It is proved by her ardent love and effort to hide herself, by having governed with happy result her whole very numerous Institute until the end of her life. It is further proved by her never having given way in her fervor, not even in the times of aridity of spirit which it also pleased the Lord to send her; in a word, her heroism is proved by all that I have narrated»100.

Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, witness V at the Roman Process, also testifies:

«As to the degree that the Servant of God reached in the exercise of all the theological and cardinal virtues and of the others of which I have spoken, I believe I can assert calmly that the Servant of God reached a degree far superior to that reached by the other sisters commonly esteemed very virtuous. And by the manner and the constancy with which the Servant of God exercised them, I believe I can likewise assure that she exercised them as a true saint, or saint of the altar, that is, as well as and even better than many saints whose lives I have heard read, and therefore in a heroic degree»101.

Sr. A. Santina Solenghi, witness VIII at the Roman Process, adds:

«As far as I know, the Servant of God, in the theological virtues as well as in the cardinal ones, and again in all the other virtues of which I have spoken, persevered until death. And in my judgment she always progressed in the exercise of those same virtues. I have already spoken of the heroism of the theological virtues. As for the cardinal ones and the others, I believe in conscience I can affirm the same, that is, that she exercised them all in a heroic degree, that is, as a saint of the altar: she exercised them in a way that had become natural to her, without effort, with ease»102.

For Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process, there is no doubt that Mother Rosa practiced the virtues in a degree above others:

«Not only do I believe that the Servant of God persevered, but I am persuaded that she always progressed in the exercise of the theological, cardinal and related virtues of which I have spoken. This is the impression I took away from the whole of her acts and her words, in dealing with her. I also heard our fellow sisters say: ‘Our Mother is becoming ever more holy’. This is my idea, my conviction, that the degree of all the above-enumerated virtues of the Servant of God was truly heroic, because she exercised them all not in a way common even to pious persons, but in an absolutely extraordinary degree, attainable only by her; in an easy, ready, unforced way, as if she possessed another nature; in a degree truly that of a saint of the altar. This is the conviction I have and assert»103.

Sr. A. Fara Martinengo, witness XV at the Roman Process, declares:

«The Servant of God exercised all the virtues as if they were innate in her and therefore in the most natural and unforced way: she exercised them in the highest degree and therefore, without hesitation, I can say that she exercised them in a heroic degree»104.

The priest Fr. Vincenzo da Alatri, witness XVIII at the Roman Process, adds:

«In all the virtues the Servant of God always remained constant and certainly never drew back, and in the love of God, which embraces all the virtues, she was always more inflamed. As to the degree of the virtues of the Servant of God, I would not know how to pronounce. Certainly she exercised them in an uncommon way and as if they were connatural to her»105.

Sr. A. Amante La Barbera, witness XXXVIII, ex officio, at the Roman Process, judges the life of Mother Rosa «wholly absorbed in the life of Jesus Christ» and therefore heroic:

«The Servant of God exercised all the virtues, without exception, in a heroic degree, that is, as if she lived a life above the senses, wholly absorbed in the life of Jesus Christ, and therefore with ease, with facility, with constancy, as if they were connatural to her, in short as all the saints whose lives I have read exercised them: and from this assertion I exclude no virtue. I would not know how to say which excelled in her, unless it be charity, which gathers all together»106.

40. — She persevered and progressed until death in the uncommon exercise of virtue: this is the conviction of Sr. A. Crocifissa Fiocchi, witness XL at the Roman Process:

«Of all the virtues, theological, cardinal and related, I have the firm conviction that the Servant of God persevered in the exercise of them until death, but that she always progressed in them. This was the impression I received when she came to visit my house: I perceived in her an increase each time. And it is also my conviction that the Servant of God practiced the above-mentioned virtues in a heroic degree: above all charity and humility; that is, that she practiced them with constancy, never drawing back before difficulties and the repugnance that sometimes it could be seen she had to overcome; with ease; in short, in a word, as I have read in the lives of many saints»107.

According to Sr. A. Giuseppina Tornatore, witness III at the Roman Process, Mother Rosa practiced the virtues «in an uncommon way, above the other sisters, themselves virtuous»:

«The Servant of God certainly exercised the virtues in an uncommon way, not only so, but also above the other sisters, themselves virtuous; she had made the habit of virtue and exercised it in a natural, spontaneous way. And if one is to argue from her penances, one must also say that her love of God was in a heroic degree»108.

Sr. A. Fara Martinengo, cited above, thus further alludes to the heroicity of Mother Rosa in the exercise of penance:

«In none of the virtues did the Servant of God ever exceed. According to our short views, it might seem to us that she exceeded in the virtue of penance and mortification, but it is clear that to her love of this virtue the Lord's helps responded, so that she not only did not make herself unfit for the office of Mother General, but not even less useful»109.

p. 47

In a manner far superior to that common among pious souls, Mother Rosa practiced the virtues, as Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, witness XX at the Roman Process, states in her testimony:

«All the aforesaid virtues, none excluded, were practiced by the Servant of God not only in a manner far superior to that common among pious souls, but with a constancy, with a facility, as if she possessed a second nature, as if they were connatural in her, as if she felt the need to act so, and not otherwise, in a heroic degree, and such as even to surpass the virtues practiced by many saints who are venerated on the altars. And this is not my opinion alone, but we always speak with this persuasion among ourselves, the sisters, and we say: ‘There will never have been another Foundress like ours!’. We admire her, but we truly do not know how to imitate her»110.

Sr. A. Fabiana Orsi, witness II at the Roman Process, not only declares that the Foundress exercised all the virtues in a heroic degree, but also that she became the living model of the rule for the Daughters of Saint Anne:

«It seems to me I can without hesitation assert that the Servant of God exercised all the virtues in a heroic degree and that in the exercise of them she never exceeded, but kept the just way proper to virtue [...]. I confirm having heard it said that all her daughters, in the 33 years she lived the life of the community, admired her as the living model of the rule, since they could not catch her transgressing even the smallest part, or departing in any act from the common method of living»111.

Sr. A. Apollonia Marchetti, witness VIII at the Naples Process, declares that Mother Rosa «exercised all the virtues in an uncommon and non-ordinary way, but extraordinary and superlative»:

«The Servant of God, as far as I know, exercised all the Christian virtues not in a common and ordinary way, but extraordinary and superlative, so as to surpass the common run of pious and virtuous souls, which means in a heroic degree [...], and this until her death. Indeed in community she was always an example of observance and of virtue, and for us sisters it was enough simply to see her to be seized with the greatest veneration for her.

I never saw, learned or read that the Servant of God, in the exercise of the Christian virtues, ever fell into any excess or exaggeration or made herself, through penances and mortifications, unfit for the discharge of her duties»112.

«She practiced the virtues constantly and in an extraordinary degree»: so Sr. A. Vittoria Archetti, witness IV of the Roman Process, expresses herself in her testimony:

p. 48

«In the exercise of all the virtues I believe, as the other sisters also think, that the Servant of God practiced them constantly, until death, without slackening. I believe that the exercise of those same virtues reached in the Servant of God an extraordinary degree, truly that of a saint, that is, as is told of the saints who are venerated on the altars»113.

41. — Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni, witness I at the Piacenza Process, is also most firmly convinced of the heroic degree in the practice of all the virtues:

«In my thinking the Servant of God exercised all the virtues in a heroic degree, in that I never saw her fail in them and also none of the rest of us practiced them in so perfect a degree. And although she exercised the above-mentioned virtues in a more perfect degree than her daughters, nevertheless she did not exceed in the exercise of them, letting herself, e.g., be dominated by immoderate zeal, or exceeding in mortification so as to make herself unable to fulfill her own offices. Thus, e.g., a few months before her death she was still going to visit the houses of the Institute»114.

The Very Rev. Fr. Stefano Ignudi, second Theological Expert, in his opinion on the writings of Mother Rosa gives this judgment on the excellent and uncommon way in which the Servant of God practiced the virtues in the course of her life:

«In scriptis omnes prodeunt virtutes, tum Theologales tum Cardinales, heroice exercitatas, quarum singularum uberrima erit seges in colligendis actibus specificis. Corusco nitent splendore (ut aliqua delibem):

— eius fides vivissima;

— spes inconcussa, altissima;

— caritas prorsus seraphica in Deum et in proximum;

— sollicitudo materna erga Sorores;

— zelus pro salute animarum;

— studium gratitudinis erga benefactores;

— humilitas sincera, profundissima;

— simplicitas cum prudentia;

— animi rectitudo;

— patientia in fere continuis infirmitatibus;

— fortitudo magnanima, insuperabilis in doloribus, adversitatibus, difficultatibus quas habuit sustinendas ab hominibus et a daemonibus;

— mortificatio, poenitentia, amor et gaudium poenalium et perpetuorum cruciatuum, incredibilia (ut vulgo dicimus);

— oratio continua, cum alta habituali elevatione in Deum;

— amor et obsequium in Ecclesiam et Apostolicam Sedem; reverentia in Episcopos, sacerdotes et religiosos;
