— pietas erga aeternum Patrem peculiaris; erga Passionem Christi et SS. Eucharistiam; erga Beatam Virginem et Sanctos; atque in subveniendo Animabus Purgatorii;

— oboedientia. Omnia fecit et scripsit, sub oboedientia superiorum et moderatorum spiritualium»115.

42. — The Very Rev. Fr. Paolino Zavarella, Expert «in re medica», in the study made on the state of normality of the Servant of God, at the request of the Congregation for the Causes of Saints, puts forward this opinion of his on the virtues practiced by Mother Rosa:

«The letters constitute a fine term of comparison: the epistolary dialogue with the Daughters is free of any artifice, maternal, concrete, edifying. The number of letters does not arouse wonder: the foundation of 358 houses, in Italy and abroad, the great administrative and disciplinary problems that had to be faced and resolved, the government of more than 4,000 sisters imposed a dense correspondence. The content of the letters and the way of expressing herself show a clear mind, a spirit that looked to the concrete and the essential. The balance, the sense of the supernatural, the concern for the spiritual good of the persons she addressed emerge with evidence»116.

The same Very Rev. Fr. Paolino Zavarella adds further:

«The psychic normality or otherwise of a subject can be ascertained by observing two important moments of his life: his behavior toward God and in relations with different persons. In this regard I wished to examine the concrete exercise of the virtues of faith and charity, in their twofold aspect toward the Creator and toward the brethren, on the part of the Servant of God; these precious elements of evaluation have made it possible to establish that faith in God and love for Him were the essential motive of Gattorno's thought and action.

The Foundress's behavior in the matter of charity toward neighbor has then made it possible to observe, in all its aspects, the whole complex of her life of relationship: and this is a basic and precious element for a judgment, because the way a subject acts in the face of the various circumstances of life, joyful or sad, painful or exhilarating, easy or difficult, lays bare his psychological state. Indeed, besides the episodes and facts that make up the fabric of daily life, one must bear in mind the great variety of persons involved with the Servant of God in the unfolding of those very facts. In all this complex of facts and persons, Gattorno's behavior always appears composed, straightforward, marked by a Christian orientation of life, always followed with persevering consistency, with a markedly supernatural vision»117.

p. 50

CHAP. V
HEROICITY OF THE VIRTUES IN PARTICULAR

43. — We are convinced that from what has been set out so far the Father Consultors are already in a position to form a judgment not only positive but flattering of the holiness and heroicity of all the virtues of the Servant of God. What has been written so far contains more than valid elements for reaching such a conclusion. The singular excellence of the virtuous habits, that is, of the whole of Mother Rosa Gattorno's working and acting in the various phases of her earthly existence, is basically revealed as patent in concrete terms.

It would therefore be superfluous to proceed to demonstrate the excellence of each virtue in particular, since the whole system of life of the Servant of God is amply based on the solid foundation of exceptional grace, of dedication to God, of self-denial, of passionate search for the divine will, of living and fiery charity for God and neighbor.

However, since it is fine and useful not only to contemplate a work of art as a whole and globally, but it is equally useful and enriching to examine its individual aspects and details, the splendor of the holiness and perfection of Mother Rosa Gattorno will, as we hope, shine all the more if we proceed to describe each of her virtues in particular.

Moreover, the constant practice in this kind of Causes and the canonical-theological requirements demand that such illustration and proof be prepared.

Obviously, the whole printed Summarium is the proof. It would suffice for the Father Consultors to read and evaluate the individual testimonies on each virtue to be convinced that each of them finds great prominence in the attestations of direct and qualified witnesses. But an Informatio has the purpose of carrying out a reasoned highlighting, a coordinated bringing to light of the material contained in the Summarium. The Informatio is a useful work, not a necessary one. Only that the Informatio cannot be imagined detached from the Summarium, that is, separated from the probative material. This is why the compilation now being prepared will inevitably be a sort of assemblage of various testimonies and documents; an assemblage which, we hope, will not be a mere juxtaposition of pieces, but rather their harmonious and reasoned composition, a sort of animation from within of the findings of the processes.

Following an order proven by practice, the Theological Virtues will be illustrated first, then the Cardinal ones, then the related Virtues.

A. THEOLOGICAL VIRTUES

44. — It is neither emphasis nor exaggeration to say that the life of Rosa Gattorno cannot be explained without Faith, Hope and Charity, which were abundantly infused in her at baptism and which found in her soul a very fertile ground, so as to bear fruit a hundredfold. Indeed, her existence, already in the years of childhood, was characterized by an extraordinary sensitivity to the divine and the supernatural, which was translated into a living desire to receive the Lord in the Eucharist, to meditate on His word, to suffer for His love, to consume herself for Him in the apostolate, to consecrate herself wholly to Him. And all this with a truly admirable perseverance, intensity, generosity and promptness, knowing neither pauses nor evasions.

1. Faith

45. — It is historically certain that all the stages of the life of our Servant of God are strikingly animated and vivified by Faith and Piety. As a child, her thoughts in germ and her spontaneous aspirations were impregnated with the sacred and the divine. And this singular capacity to attune herself to the divine did not weaken as she grew, though it acquired ever more personalized tones. With the passing of the years, far from digressions and crises of faith and piety arising in her, the Christian sense of life grew ever stronger, a life never conceived except in terms of conscious dedication: to God and to His service. Even before being a religious, already in 1856, she made a vow of perpetual fasting; on 8 December 1858, she made the perpetual vows of chastity and obedience; on 24 September 1861, she made profession as a Franciscan tertiary and chose Saint Francis of Assisi as her special patron.

Having then become a widow after 6 years of married life, she carried out her intention to consecrate herself to God in religious life and began the painful iter of the foundation of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, which was nothing other than the development, in another form, of the same existential conception of Faith of her life.

p. 52

It is therefore this straight line of Faith, which starts from childhood and ends only with death, that constitutes a first and solid argument for defining the habit of Faith of Mother Rosa Gattorno as heroic. From the procedural records emerge numerous demonstrative arguments of a Faith which Mother Gattorno exercised supra communem operandi modum: they are proofs of particular value because the witnesses drew them from their own personal observation and show, evidently, that the first theological virtue informed her whole life.

The first finding made in studying the life and work of Mother Rosa is that everything in her: her spirituality, her apostolate, the foundation of the Institute, the reason, in short, of her whole long existence, was Christian faith generously and heroically lived to its ultimate demands. Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, witness XX at the Roman Process, testifies:

«The Servant of God used to say that God had set her Faith in diamond, so deeply did she feel it in her heart and alive. I heard her say many times that she would be ready to give her blood for the faith»118.

Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process, expresses herself in the same sense:

«The Servant of God always told us that God had set her Faith in diamond, so alive and deep did she feel it. I heard her say: ‘Oh, if only it were given me to shed my blood for the faith!’. The speech of the Servant of God in her exhortations, in her conferences, was always this: to stand firm in the faith and to be attached to the Holy See. If anyone had allowed himself some criticism of the Pope, she interrupted, declaring that she did not want to hear, because, when it comes to the Pope, all is well; no criticism or opposition must be admitted»119.

Sr. A. Fara Martinengo, witness XV at the Roman Process, adds:

«Beginning with Faith, the Servant of God was a burning torch, continual, living, most living. She had no other ideal than God and his glory. I myself heard her, speaking in a special way to the sisters who were leaving for the missions, exhort them with burning words to be ready to give even life and blood for the faith. Once she was ill. She came to the novitiate, when I too was there, and when she spoke of the faith it seemed that every symptom of illness had vanished from her; indeed she seemed rejuvenated.

She seemed the perpetual companion of the Nazarene in teaching the catechism. I myself heard her, even in the parlor, never neglect any occasion to teach and instruct about our faith»120.

p. 53

Sr. A. Michelina Negri, witness X at the Roman Process, testifies:

«The Servant of God not only believed firmly, but I myself heard her exclaim: ‘Oh, if only I were given an occasion to shed my blood for the Faith!’, and she exhorted the sisters and novices to have the same sentiments. In the things of our Faith she was extremely well instructed, and when she went to the novitiate to give conferences, we too went, and it seemed to us we were hearing a preacher. Her conferences dealt either with some point of the rule or with the catechism. She also questioned us to see whether we had understood and were instructed on our duties and on the catechism, showing that her great concern was that the sisters be instructed in the catechism in order to be able to instruct others. She wanted the local superiors of the other houses too to give similar conferences to their sisters, and she herself gave them when she went on visitation»121

4. His Eminence Cardinal Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process, brings out well the importance and dynamic presence of theological faith in the life and work of Mother Rosa. Here is his fine deposition:

«As regards Faith, (Mother Rosa) adhered with perfect attachment to all the truths revealed and proposed by the Church, and I do not doubt that she would have come to shed her blood for any one of them. Such living faith moved her to take the initiative of sending her sisters to Africa for the conversion of unbelievers and schismatics. This moved her to pray for the conversion of sinners and of unbelievers and schismatics, to pay with her person and with her blood for the faults of others, torturing her body. This faith again moved her to declare herself unworthy of being so favored by Him:

The foundation of her Institute, dedicated to religious instruction, education, care of the sick, care of abandoned girls, was from a principle of faith. The thought of the presence of God dominated her to such a degree that she remained — I would say — absorbed, and to me myself she sometimes declared that especially after communion her union with God was very close, and sometimes when she went to confession, at the moment of absolution she no longer heard the priest's words, raised as if outside herself by the thought of the goodness of God. And this last fact she told me to quiet her conscience, for fear of not having been present to herself for the effects to be obtained in absolution»122.

46. — Among the most evident manifestations of the theological Faith of the Servant of God, her spirit of prayer and of intimate union with God stands out eminently. Mother Rosa Gattorno realized in her life the warm recommendation of the Second Vatican Council to consecrated souls in the Decree Perfectae Caritatis:

«Let them assiduously cultivate the spirit of prayer and prayer itself, drawing them from the genuine sources of Christian spirituality»123.

Sr. A. Michelina Negri declares in this regard:

«The Servant of God possessed the spirit of prayer in an eminent degree, and inspired it in us too. She never wasted time: either she worked or she prayed. She prayed in all the time that remained free to her, and also at night, being unable to rest because of her ailments, she prayed. We sisters know it, because when she was worse, one of us staying to watch over her, we saw that she prayed. And even when she was not made worse by her illness, she sometimes said, with indifference, and in a way that evidently showed she was not speaking out of vanity: ‘Last night I could not sleep, and so I said to myself fifteen decades of the rosary, a hundred Requiem aeternam, etc.

It was plain to see that the Servant of God, when she prayed, was in the presence of God. Especially after Communion, for which she spent no less than an hour of thanksgiving kneeling on the floor, she was seen so absorbed and motionless that she seemed not even to feel it if one went to shake her or question her; she seemed not to hear [...].

It was seen that the Servant of God was always in the presence of the Lord, as appeared from her words, her look, her demeanor, not only to us sisters but also to outsiders who had occasion to speak with her, whom I often heard say: ‘But your Mother is a124 saint!»

A woman of deep interior life, Mother Rosa lived habitually in the presence of God. Prayer, joined to meditation and contemplation, was her existential atmosphere. On this aspect Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process, testifies:

«How she prayed, the Servant of God! Besides her meditation in the morning, in Piacenza in her free hours she went up to her little secret room, and there she prayed, as could be understood very well from her expressions, such as these: ‘Oh, I am going up there to collect myself and lift myself up a little!» And when she came down, you should have seen her, how radiant she was; she had a face of Paradise; and I was quite content when I knew that she was withdrawing or had withdrawn to her cell, because I would have the pleasure of contemplating her face, which instilled something celestial in my soul.

At night, as she declared, she slept little, and ‘I spend my hours in prayer and meditation’, she added. Here in Rome, when she had an hour free, she went to the chapel, and sometimes locked herself in there so as not to be disturbed. In the last years, despite her sufferings, her thoughts were more there than here. For me her union with God was continual, and this union appeared manifest even to those who came to visit her. They were all enchanted to find themselves before this wholly humble person, who spoke little and was wholly submissive. When they left they said to us: ‘Oh, what a Mother you have!’, and they made it understood that they had conceived of her an esteem as of an extraordinary woman»125.

Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, witness V at the Roman Process, testifies in these terms on Mother Rosa's spirit of prayer:

«When the Servant of God prayed, her face and her whole person took on such a bearing that she seemed an angel. She did not answer anyone who called her, especially in the prayers before and after Mass, and during meditation. In the chapel she used to kneel at a kneeler; but after communion she remained on her knees always on the bare ground, leaning on a chair, for the space of an hour, and this every time she went to the chapel, even when ill in the last times. The prayer of the Servant of God, as I said, was, one may say, continual; she prayed in the chapel and she prayed in her own room by day and by night. Often she prayed in her own room, called me to keep her company and we prayed together»126.

47. — The spirit of prayer being one of the most notable characteristics of the exercise of faith in Mother Rosa, she had become among her daughters an excellent teacher, and on this aspect of her teaching Sr. A. Fara Martinengo, witness XV, testifies at the Roman Process:

«On prayer she used all the most effective comparisons to urge her sisters to persist in it and to fall in love with it, and so be able, in the hidden life, to taste the beauties of faith: ‘Prayer is the door of Paradise’ — she used to repeat —; ‘prayer is the key that opens the door of the Heart of Jesus; prayer is also the voice that makes you feel whether you have observed the holy rule’. So one day I said to her: ‘So, Mother, prayer is the panacea for all ills’. ‘Oh’ — the Servant of God replied — ‘you may well say so, prayer is the remedy of all ills, but it is also the reward for what you would like to have with greater perfection’.

In the conferences that the Servant of God came to give to the novitiate and to the superiors during the General Chapter, I remember that they almost always dealt with the observance of some point of the rule, supported by prayer: ‘Take care, daughters — she said — in joy, in sorrow, in trials, in work, always lean on prayer’»127.

On this same subject the great friend and confidante of Mother Rosa, Princess of Fitalia, Emilia Settimo, witness XXXI at the Roman Process, expresses herself thus:

«To begin with faith I shall say that in her there was the kind that moves mountains, and she communicated it to others [...]. Her life was a continual prayer day and night. Even when she spoke with me, I often noticed that her soul was united to God completely and always. She recommended prayer to everyone and with me she insisted on meditation»128.

Sr. A. Vittoria Archetti, witness IV at the Roman Process, declares:

«She held prayer in the highest esteem, and by example and word urged us to the exercise of it. When she prayed, she was seen wholly absorbed in God; and faith and fervor shone great in her bearing [...]. She was always seen recollected in herself, and showed her spirit always ready for prayer, as I saw myself in the various months of my stays in Rome»129.

48. — The devotions to the Most Holy Trinity, to the Passion of the Lord, to the Eucharist, to Our Lady, to Saint Anne and to several other Saints are one of the finest manifestations and precious fruits of Mother Rosa's most profound faith, cultivated by her with loving fidelity throughout her whole life.

Cardinal Granito di Belmonte, witness I at the Roman Process, testifies:

«A special and characteristic devotion of the Servant of God was that to the Eternal Father, to whom she always turned with filial trust, and in the Institute devotion and a prayer to the Eternal Father are prescribed. Ardent was her devotion to the Most Holy Sacrament [...]. She made visits to Him as frequently as she could, and sought as she could to extend His cult in her Institute. When she had the opportunity, she heard a second Mass besides that of the community. During the thanksgiving she made for communion she was not infrequently rapt from her senses, remaining motionless. When she foresaw that she would be rapt outside herself, she hurried to leave the chapel and withdraw to her room.

Particular also was the devotion of the Servant of God to the Crucifix: to Him she had recourse in all her difficulties and anxieties, often having on her lips the words: ‘My Crucifix will see to it, will help me, etc.’ [...]. From her Crucifix the Servant of God had experienced ample comforts and spiritual helps, especially in the most difficult moments for the Institute and in her interior struggles and those with demons [...]. When someone had recourse to her, asking for the help of her prayers, she ordinarily answered: ‘I shall tell my Crucifix’. In short, her Crucifix was for her the anchor in all the storms by which she was assailed. In a word, it was her all»130.

On Mother Rosa's devotion to the Passion of the Lord, several witnesses hand down many and very beautiful accounts. Among these, since it is impossible to cite them all, we present that of Sr. A. Vittoria Archetti, witness IV at the Roman Process:

«Immense was her devotion to the Passion of the Lord, which she always had present in her thought, and for this she loved with all her heart the Crucifix which she called hers, and she closed her letters saying: ‘I leave you in my Crucifix’. In tribulations she turned to Him and presented Him to us as a model of resignation in our anguish, and as an object of comfort and hope. A sister of mine in the flesh who died in America, a religious in our house in Pernambuco, told me: ‘Do you know, Sister Vittoria? I asked the Mother General to have my portrait made and she answered me: The portrait you have: Look at the Crucifix!’ [...].

She was most devoted also to the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus, whose devotion she inculcated, and she wanted us to consecrate the month of June to Him and for Him she invited us to make sacrifices too. When occasion arose, she inculcated this devotion also on the people and the girls (as also that of the Passion of Our Lord) and in a special way the devotion of the first Fridays of the month»131.

The Princess of Fitalia, witness XXXI at the Roman Process, adds:

«The Servant of God never wrote a letter without naming her Crucifix and closing it with Him. In every conversation with me she brought in her Crucifix. The Crucifix was her life. In Holy Week one may say she was no longer of this earth: on Good Friday she shut herself in her room and no one saw her»132.

49. — In the life of Mother Rosa her great devotion to Jesus Crucified is intimately bound to the eucharistic mystery in its threefold aspect of sacrifice, sacrament and continual presence in the tabernacle. Indeed the Acts of the Process are full of allusions to Mother Rosa's great devotion to the Eucharist. Sr. Fabiana Orsi, witness II at the Roman Process, recalls:

«Great was her devotion to the Most Holy Sacrament. In church she was seen motionless, and no noise managed to distract her during any exercise of piety. She received communion every day and prolonged her acts of thanksgiving at length. The Servant of God could do this because she heard Mass in the chapel on the first floor together with her secretaries and did not go down to the church of Saint Anne with the whole community, perhaps because she was always suffering in health. Communion was so dear to her that never any day did she wish to leave it, neither on account of any grave infirmity, nor by reason of the strain of journeys, on which she preferred to remain fasting until after twelve so as not to deprive herself of holy Communion»133.

Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, witness V at the Roman Process, declares:

«Most devoted to the Eucharist, every day without fail she received communion and as far as I know she never left it on any day. She herself told me that even as a laywoman she had never left off daily Communion. She did not mind sacrifices in order to receive communion. If necessary she stopped somewhere, before reaching the end of her journey, in order to receive communion. She sent word ahead by letters and telegrams to the houses where she was to arrive so that a priest would be found for her to receive communion [...].

Sometimes in the last times of her life, and sometimes also by reason of travel, she could not hear Mass; but at times it was celebrated for her in her room adjoining her bedroom, so that she could hear it without too much inconvenience, and on those occasions she rose from bed and took those few steps to go into the other room to hear Mass. This happened few times and especially on Sundays. Long and most diligent was the preparation of the Servant of God for holy Communion, and the thanksgiving lasted at least an hour. When she made Communion immediately after midnight, after receiving the sacred host, she signed to me to go away, and I returned at four in the morning, and even then I found her in prayer [...].

She exhorted her sisters to receive communion daily whenever the occasion presented itself, and especially in her visit to the houses, and I too heard her say to them: ‘A sister who does not receive Jesus has nothing in herself. When some religious came from outside and arrived before eleven in the morning, she asked them whether they were still fasting, and whether they were willing to make Communion, and exhorted them to make it if the confessor was still at home at that hour, and several times she sent me to see whether he was there [...].

She also saw to it that her religious made frequent spiritual communions. She said to the novices: ‘You have made few, but you will have made them well, is it not so? Tomorrow you will make a few more and always well’. She suggested to them the most fitting way to make spiritual Communion and useful thoughts for it. For example she said to them: ‘Here at home we always revolve around Jesus in the Sacrament; if we go up the stairs we have close by the chapel where Jesus is in the Tabernacle; if we go on the terrace to walk or hang out the washing or do other work, the windows of the church where Jesus is in the Sacrament are close by. Everything, in short, invites us to unite ourselves to Him and urges us to spiritual Communion. Everything in the house recalls us to Jesus, and we ought to be like the seraphim of love. And how could we not unite ourselves to Him spiritually?’»134.

50. — Eminent too in the Servant of God was the most ardent devotion she nourished toward Our Lady. Among the many testimonies in this regard we present the following in outline:

From Cardinal Granito di Belmonte:

«Most particular was the devotion of the Servant of God to the Most Holy Virgin. She nourished a special cult of her Immaculate Conception. In all the prayers she addressed to her God the Servant of God never failed to join the intercession of the Most Holy Virgin»135.

From the Princess of Fitalia:

«She nourished devotion, love and filial trust, altogether extraordinary, toward Our Lady, as I saw from her speeches and her writings»136.

From Sr. A. Serafina Foglia:

«She prescribed to her Institute, besides the daily rosary, the little chaplet of the Immaculate and that of Our Lady of Sorrows; she added to these the office of Our Lady. On Saturdays, for this devotion, she had eucharistic benediction given in the public church and in the chapel adjoining here. She was so devoted to the Immaculate of Lourdes that she was not content until she found the benefactress who would make for her in our public church a facsimile of the grotto of Lourdes. She also wanted Our Lady of Lourdes in all her houses, where possible, and in those houses where there were not sufficient means, she provided directly herself»137.

As regards the sincere devotion that Mother Rosa nourished also for Saint Anne, testimonies likewise abound. Sr. A. Fara Martinengo testifies:

«Joined to that of Our Lady was the dutiful devotion she paid to Saint Anne, our Mother, and she wanted it paid also by her sisters. Her cult of Saint Anne was so ardent and communicative that we felt stimulated to imitate her»138.

Sr. A. Serafina Foglia declares:

«That the Servant of God was most devoted to Saint Anne there is no need to say. The very name given to her Institute attests it, the prayers and practices prescribed to the Institute by the Servant of God in her honor [...]. To her she attributed so many graces she had received for her religious. To her, in a particular way, she recommended her religious who went to America: ‘Saint Anne — she said to her sisters — is our Foundress, and to her we must always commend ourselves, and she will not abandon us; she will guide us, extricate us from the difficulties from which we would not know how to extricate ourselves; she will free us from dangers’»139.

The witnesses also proclaim very often in the Acts of the Process the sincere and cordial piety of Mother Rosa, born from the root of her great faith, toward Saint Joseph, Saint Michael, Saint Francis of Assisi, Saint Francis of Paola, etc.:

«These were the saints to whom she principally turned with trust and, I would say, familiarity in her needs»140.

51. — But an aspect that strikes one deeply in the life of heroic faith of Mother Rosa is the vision she had of the Church, Mystical Body of Jesus. To this aspect of Mother Rosa's life of faith the Very Rev. Fr. Lázaro Iriarte devotes a chapter in his study on the spirituality of the Servant of God:

«The profound sense of Church of Rosa Gattorno would deserve a separate treatise. It is not only submission to the representatives of the hierarchical Church, but a true ecclesial spirituality inspired by faith and nourished by veneration and love. Having grown up in a family environment where she had to deal with Freemasons and anticlericals, she had to mature from youth her fidelity to mother Church, a fidelity that became service and apostolic activity, seeking from the beginning to make sure of the authenticity of her initiatives through the approval and guidance of the diocesan authority.

It was obedience to the archbishop of Genoa, Msgr. Charvaz, that made her accept, in 1864, at the insistent request of the Servant of God Fr. Giuseppe Frassinetti, first the presidency of the Daughters of Mary and then the office of superior of the nascent Pious Union of the Daughters of Mary Immaculate, the new Ursulines. And it was the same archbishop who verified the genuineness of the divine impulse that urged her to found a new Institute and encouraged her to go personally to Pope Pius IX to make sure, from the lips of the supreme Pastor, that this was the will of God»141.

Precisely because she saw in the Church the mystery of the Risen Christ prolonged through the centuries, Mother Rosa Gattorno, driven by her faith, felt solidarity with all who formed the Mystical Body of Jesus, hierarchy and believing people, shepherds and sheep of the flock that the Good Shepherd wishes to lead to the fertile pastures of eternal life.

Cardinal Gennaro Granito di Belmonte testifies:

«Profound was always her veneration for the Supreme Pontiff. Toward Pius IX, however, to her veneration out of faith she joined particular affection and devotion. Full of respect and veneration she was likewise toward anyone who bore the priestly character»142.

Extraordinary was the veneration that Mother Rosa nourished in her heart toward Pope Pius IX, as the Princess of Fitalia, Emilia Settimo, recalls in her testimony:

«She was moreover extraordinarily devoted to the Holy See: every order or wish that came from there was for her divine law, and for this her suffering over the Apostolic Visitation was the greater. Needless to say how great was her devotion in particular to Pius IX, who was for her like a saint in heaven; he was her protector, her director, and everything; and Pius IX had a great affection for her. She told me that once, going to an audience, and other persons being present, Pius IX turned at once to her, who had placed herself in a corner behind the others. In telling me this, she also told me of her great confusion then and of the immense condescension Pius IX showed her. Pius IX, joking, called her his ragamuffin»143.

Relations with the representatives of the Church, beyond the persons, were of great respect and veneration:

«Although she had to suffer from various bishops, she never failed in her devotion even toward them»144.

«The faith of the Servant of God extended to everything the Church teaches, and it was most lively, as can be seen not only from the instructions and exhortations she gave the sisters, but above all from the love she had for suffering»145.

«Particular also was her veneration for her confessors and also for her directors, though from these she did not always receive satisfactory answers to her questions, as regards communications made to her by the Lord, by which her spirit remained in anguish; the Servant of God, however, received these anguishes as a trial from the Lord, and the sentiment of veneration for those who directed her did not weaken in her at all [...]. The Servant of God therefore suffered (because of this veneration of hers toward any ecclesiastic) when, for the good running of the houses, or to remedy some inconvenience that had arisen, she saw herself obliged to take measures that could redound to the discredit of some priest. Here, I repeat, she took such measures with all delicacy and prudence, so that the honor of the priests might not be harmed»146.

52. — In the teaching of the Servant of God we note Mother Rosa's insistence that all the religious of the Institute may find in faith the foundation of their spiritual life and the starting point toward the highest peaks of perfection. She writes, for example, to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa:

«(the Daughters of Saint Anne) carry (the Eternal Father) continually on their lips and in all their actions invoke Him, keep Him in their hearts because they love Him as Father, placing in Him all their good; they adore Him in His most high dignity, in His divinity they learn every delight; finally you can well say: ‘they are the true daughters of my Eternal Father; because they expect everything from Him and rest in Him alone’; my Jesus, is this not true, and could your heart delay in coming to the aid of what these creatures need and in particular of the one who more than all is in need, His slave?»147.

For reasons of faith she invites her religious to seek the transcendent and to desire «those goods that God alone can give»:

«Come, let us leave these earthly things, let us lift our minds on high and seek to have and desire those goods that God alone can give. And these are the only ones that we shall possess for an eternity, as I so desire it for all and I pray that these words of mine addressed to you may have the fortune of bearing good fruits, all to the glory of God and honor of our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of Mary Immaculate»148.

Mother Rosa seeks to transmit to her religious that most ardent faith which was always at the base of her aspirations and her works:

«Come, courage, soon you will see that the Lord will console you, but an ounce of patience and two of faith in God and you will have everything, I assure you, but peace and little fussing, day by day embrace the cross the Lord sends us, remember that new days, new crosses»149.

2. Hope

53. — To express in words of genuine biblical flavor the habit of outstanding Hope of the Servant of God, with all its baggage of detachment from earth, of aspirations to Heaven, of full trust in God, of serenity in trials, etc., the expressions of Saint Paul to the Christians of Colossae fit very aptly:

«Quae sursum sunt quaerite, ubi Christus est in dextera Dei sedens, quae sursum sunt sapite, non quae super terram. Mortui enim estis, et vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo»150.

One of the key messages of Mother Rosa's earthly story is the lesson of other-worldliness proper to the believer, especially the Christian. In the great — and almost exclusive — talk that is made today of earthliness, of «human» experience, the life of Mother Rosa Gattorno stands there, one might say, crying out the other-worldly vocation, the call to the things that «sursum sunt». The supernatural outlook was present in Mother Rosa already in the years of childhood, adolescence and youth, of marriage and then always during the experience of religious life. And it is clear that perseverance of very many years in this outlook, with the whole series of concrete renunciations and achievements of good for neighbor, implies in itself an innumerable series of acts of trust, of abandonment to God, of fidelity to the providential plan of the Lord, of resistance to and overcoming of purely human calculations.

Cardinal Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, in his testimony at the

p. 63

Roman Process, gives us the synthesis of the theological Hope practiced by the Servant of God in the course of her earthly experience:

«In all her life all her work was always directed to pleasing God in this life, and then to possessing Him forever in the other. This hope she also transfused into her religious while she was forming them, to whom she always pointed to paradise as the final goal. In herself, however, she had nothing of confidence, but it was all placed in the blood and the merits of Jesus.

Not only was she resigned in all the trials she had to suffer, which were moreover continual, but she received them with generosity of soul, recognized them as deserved by her unworthiness; I do not know whether she ever prayed that they be lightened for her, but she always showed herself in this perfectly conformed to the will of God, convinced that the trials came to her for her demerits; the stronger such trials were, the more she raged against herself with penances, seeking to appease the Lord. In these circumstances of trial, she sometimes wrote to me, and several times spoke to me in person, asking to be allowed to use her harsh penances, that is, the discipline to blood.

Knowing that this harmed her physically, given the continual fasts and the other penances that she also continually made, I was reluctant to grant it, but her thirst to suffer was so great and she knew how to manifest it to me so well, that I saw myself obliged to give way in part.

From temporal things she was perfectly detached and her heart never ran after money. For the needs of the Institute, however, she did not hesitate to go begging, and, made strong by her unlimited trust in the Lord, she met all the humiliations that are encountered in such circumstances. God, however, amply compensated the humiliations she had in these begging rounds, providing for her very often more than the urgent need. Although she made use of men, her exclusive trust was nevertheless in God, considering these only as ministers of His spiritual or temporal providence.

When the local superiors of any of her houses laid their difficulties before her, she directed them straight to the Lord, seeking to instill in them the most unlimited trust in Him. I remember well that in the early days of her foundation in Naples, her Religious, worn out by the toil of caring for the sick day and night, and increasing in number to meet the ever greater requests for assistance, often appealed to the Servant of God to provide them with lodging more suited to their religious life, and also to hygiene; for it must be noted that at first in Naples they had no house of their own, but lived in rented quarters. The habitual answer of the Servant of God was constantly this: ‘Have trust in God: He will provide for us’»151.

54. — This was the iter of hope heroically lived by the Servant of God. We now see abundantly confirmed by other witnesses, point by point, what was described by His Eminence Cardinal Granito di Belmonte.

Sr. M. Teresa Patti di Sorrentino, witness VI at the Palermo Process, expresses herself thus:

«In all the time that I knew her I noticed in her a living trust in the assistance of the Lord in all the works she undertook for the good, the growth and the erection of the various houses of the Institute. Nor ever, I can affirm in conscience, did I see her fail in spirit and strength in succeeding in the holy undertaking that for the glory of God she had set herself. Moreover I am convinced that on this hope, on the powerful help of God, the sublime inspirations of her good works were founded, in order to win as reward holy paradise. All her cares were directed to the acquisition of eternal beatitude and for this she consecrated to God her soul, her life, her possessions.

For this hope she abandoned everything to follow the voice of Jesus, breaking the most sacred earthly affections of daughter and mother. She leaps over the body of her mother who, although a woman of strong piety, hindered her in her holy purposes. She flees from her father's house to please God.

The Mother always hoped in divine help and not in human aids, as she herself told me several times. She then inculcated this hope in God in everyone, especially the sisters, by word and in writing.

The Mother, in acting, always had in view pleasing God and acquiring holy paradise [...]. She had in God an unlimited confidence, and much more did her trust in Him grow amid the disillusionments from creatures. Several times, seeing her assailed on all sides and even betrayed by persons she had benefited, I asked her how she could still have trust: ‘I have trust in my Jesus, and that is enough for me’, she answered. I never saw her lose heart in any adverse circumstance; on the contrary, in the most unforeseen and difficult cases she reacted with a supernatural strength, and at these moments more than ever she had recourse to prayer. And I several times in these circumstances saw her come out of the chapel, tranquil as if nothing sinister had ever happened, smiling in her conformity to the divine wills»152.

The Very Rev. Msgr. Angelo Raffaele Covino, sole witness at the Additional Process of Teggiano, testifies:

«I have a high idea of the Christian hope that animated the Servant of God: she had no earthly aims, no attachments or concerns for temporal things: all her aspirations were for God and for eternal goods. In struggles, anguishes or contradictions, all her trust was in God and in her Crucifix, as she expressed it: and this she always insinuated to her religious, not to trust in human aids but to have recourse to Jesus in the Sacrament, to Jesus Crucified, and to go forward with calm and tranquility»153.

On the outstanding hope of Mother Rosa the «profile offered us by Sr. A. Fabiana Orsi, witness II at the Roman Process, is also very complete and detailed:

«The soul of the Servant of God was turned toward heaven, and I never heard from her mouth, nor heard it said by others, that she said any word of mistrust in this regard. Sometimes she also said to me: ‘Everything is obtained from God: have trust in God and you will lack nothing.

In her tribulations her refuge was prayer; her hope, however, was wholly placed in the wounds and merits of Jesus Crucified. She received tribulations from God with great humility and gratitude, as a great good.

Her heart was totally averse to honors; she suffered even at being called Mother General and did not want the title of Mother General to be put on letters addressed to her. When her daughters, receiving her in their houses, honored her with acts of reverence, I did not notice on her face any sign of satisfaction; rather she was seen to be altogether indifferent. Likewise her heart did not go after riches, and I never saw her discouraged, nor heard it said that anyone ever saw her discouraged for lack of money, as sometimes happened at the beginning of the foundation of her Institute, when at times even the necessary was lacking. In financial straits, however, she had help that arrived providentially. In these straits, however, the Servant of God made special prayers and ordered others for her sisters. When she had special needs, in Piacenza she shut herself in her room under the roof set aside for penances, and there did violence to the Lord. Likewise here in Rome in her needs, of whatever kind they were, she was in the habit of shutting herself in her room to pray and do penances.

This trust in God she did not keep for herself alone, but transfused it also into her religious, and also into other afflicted and troubled persons»154.

55. — At the Naples Process, Sr. A. Apollonia Marchetti, witness VIII, presents this fine deposition on the heroic hope of Mother Rosa:

«Concerning Christian Hope I testify that the life of the Servant of God was so informed by virtue as to show that she always thought of the attainment of eternal salvation and of the means to arrive at it. She held temporal things in no account, from which she lived entirely detached, and I can say that in everything there was contempt for herself. She never kept anything special for herself and took from the community exclusively the bare necessity; indeed we sisters were obliged to change her habits or other effects always in secret, because the Servant of God did not want new habits.

The exemplarity of her life is proof that the Servant of God embraced the religious state by divine vocation and devoted herself to the foundation of the Institute for the sole glory of God. The difficulty of the undertaking appears greater if one considers that she devoted herself to the foundation of the Institute in times of political upheaval, while cloisters and convents were being arbitrarily closed. In any temporal anguish the Servant of God always showed herself trusting in divine Providence»155.

That the trust the Servant of God had placed in the Lord was admirable and extraordinary as the ripe and precious fruit of her outstanding Hope is confirmed to us by Sr. A. Giuseppina Tornatore, witness III at the Roman Process:

«It never occurred to me that the trust of the Servant of God was excessive, but that although she sometimes undertook works with scanty means, she was seen very soon to be helped by the Lord, nor have I ever heard that other sisters or even persons outside the Institute accused the Servant of God of being imprudent or excessive in her trust. I must also add that she sought to instill this trust in us, her daughters, and exhorted us all to hope and trust in the Lord»156.

56. — Practicing the virtue of Hope in a heroic degree, she sought to form her daughters firmly on the foundation of this theological virtue, as is deduced from the deposition of Sr. A. Cunegonda Pacini, witness VI at the Naples Process:

«Many times in her simplicity she drew our attention to her sufferings, showing that she was all swollen, but at the same time full of jubilation, raising her eyes to heaven she exclaimed: ‘All for my Jesus, and then she repeated the words of Saint Francis: ‘So great is the good I expect that every pain is a delight to me’. She therefore lived detached from the things of earth and in order to attend better to the salvation of her soul chose religious life. In all difficulties, whether for the foundation of our Institute, a certainly arduous work, or for the maintenance and development of that Institute, the Servant of God never lost her full and entire trust in God, whose Providence she therefore always had occasion to experience. Such trust she moreover had in everything she undertook, and she therefore sought to insinuate it also in us sisters. She had to suffer some aridity of spirit and the proof of it is that, having sometimes had recourse to the Servant of God because I felt little fervor, she answered me: ‘Ah, if you knew! Your mother also suffers from these obscurities; but one must not lose heart, they are trials that God sends us! The saints too were subject to them’»157.

Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, witness V at the Roman Process, thus completes the picture of the Hope heroically practiced by Mother Rosa:

«She often spoke of Paradise and desired it, and awaited it through the merits of Jesus Christ and said: ‘By our own merits we shall certainly not get there’. Yet she did not want our soul to be attached chiefly to Paradise, but to the love of Jesus, and she said to us her daughters: ‘We religious must try to love Jesus much and ever more, not because He gives us Paradise, but He will certainly give it to us if we love Him’. She did not want, in short, a self-interested love toward Jesus, but a generous love, and she gave us the example of Saint Teresa, of whom she told that, met one day by her sisters with a bucket of water in one hand and a lighted torch in the other, and asked what she was going to do, she answered:

p. 67

‘With this water I am going to put out hell and with this torch to burn paradise’, meaning by this that she did not want paradise and hell to exist before the eyes of her nuns as a motive for doing good and avoiding evil, but only Jesus infinitely lovable. She never placed her heart in the things of this world. She felt a most lively repugnance for money, and it was for her a great sacrifice, as she told me, to handle it, and so as not to handle it, she did not keep it, she wanted me to keep it. She therefore spoke the truth when she asserted she had no money (and this she happened to say especially with relatives), and she spoke the truth equally when she said she always had enough money and did not know what to do with it. For wealth she never looked anyone in the face, and her affection for the Princess of Fitalia had no motive in the latter's wealth. She said that Jesus had never let her lack the necessary money. She never sought comforts and said: ‘We must not seek to be well, but rather to be unwell’. Expecting everything from God, she did not become alarmed or agitated. In every sort of tribulation she never lost heart, having all her trust in God, saying: ‘It is He who inspires the people of this world to come to our aid’. When it seems to us that our affairs are going badly, we should then go and thank the Lord, since, God wanting it so, we too must be content.

Sometimes she said: ‘When our affairs turn out badly, we must be content and thank the Lord, because by this He wants to test our faith, and then He will come to our aid. The saints were content when things went badly for them, and so we too must do’. She sought to instill trust and hope in God in her sisters, and also in every sort of troubled and afflicted person. She then told her sisters who went to assist the sick that they should not lend themselves only for temporal care, but should comfort in every way, pointing to the hope of supernatural goods. I heard her many times comfort the poor with good words, speaking to them of God and of eternal goods and of resignation. ‘We must love Jesus — she said to them — seek Jesus, and He will never let us lack anything’. When poor people presented themselves, complaining that they lacked everything, she said to them: ‘This is the sign that you do not love Jesus enough. Love Him and He will not let you lack anything’. I recall that at the Villa Pontellini in Fiesole, where I was on holiday with the Servant of God, many poor people came and some of them in poor health. The Servant of God gave them alms with her own hands, accompanying them with holy words of comfort and resignation. And I recall that two or three persons went away cured, as I saw them come to thank the Mother because they were cured. I further recall that the Servant of God said to them: ‘Thank God and Saint Anne’»158.

57. — Among so many other testimonies, we finally present this one of Sr. A. Michelina Negri, witness X at the Roman Process:

«Who can doubt that the Servant of God had and exercised also the virtue of Hope? She expected nothing from this world, and all her hope was placed in God. ‘Even with us religious — she told us — the devil tries to gain some advantage, soliciting our heart to attach itself to the things of this earth, but remember that all is vanity and affliction of spirit, and that we can expect everything only from God.

In all difficulties she was resigned to the wills of God, to whom she turned in prayer: ‘Thy will be done’. This was her habitual motto in sorrows and in difficulties; and when something went awry for us, she exhorted us to abandon ourselves to the wills of God. And if we complained that we had not been heard after many prayers, she said to us: ‘It is a sign that it is not good for your soul that this thing go according to your plans’. She had no attachment to her ideas and her will, but showed herself very submissive and deferential in everything to her superiors.

Despite her unlimited trust in God, however, she made use of human means, and in difficulties she did not strive to escape them, but abandoned herself to God. Her trust in the Providence of God was rewarded by the Lord even in a prodigious way. ‘Abandon yourselves to the Providence of God — she told us — and you will never lack anything’. And this abandonment she suggested also to persons outside, or desolate, or poor, or afflicted in any way»159.

The theological Hope of Mother Rosa being so living and profound, it became for her daughters a true model to imitate. She herself writes to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa:

«I assure you that this poor Mother of yours shares in your afflictions, but I would like you to be my imitator in courage and in confidence in God, sole object of our works because for Him alone we do everything and from Him alone we want the pay, never from men»160.

For her Hope is «an anticipated paradise» and in this sense she expresses herself writing to the same Sr. A. Francesca Camisa:

«Courage, then, and all confidence in the good God; if you do so you will enjoy an anticipated paradise»161

At Christmas 1868 she gave this lesson of hope to Caterina Rapallino:

«My dear, and to arrive at this (communion with God) look at the dear Child Jesus: he wants us to become little girls and to grow only in Him and He wants to grow in us, giving us his food and strengthening us with the precious wine of his blood; for this He wants us to live in this life so as then to arrive in his presence with the purple robe of his most divine blood enameled, and, my daughter, this purple we cannot have unless we climb the cross»162.

p. 69

In Christian hope Mother Rosa finds the finest motives for accepting not only with resignation but also with joy the sufferings of life. So she expresses herself in a most beautiful letter to her friend and confidante, the Princess of Fitalia, on the occasion of the serene and Christian death of a dear relative:

«What a beautiful grace: he did not even notice he was dying! Oh, blessed soul, who had so great a privilege! Confession and Communion, and then he fell asleep in the Lord! What a great grace, Emilia, are you weeping? It is true that you have lost him, but for an eternity you will possess him»163.

To Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni she gives this prudent counsel:

«My dear daughter, do not trouble yourself over anything, all confidence in God, everything in the light of this is nothing»164.

3. Charity toward God

58. — Benedict XIV, in reporting the signs that indicate, according to the various ascetical authors, the presence of the love of God in a person, then makes of them a compendium as follows:

— thoughts continually turned to God; — frequent and pious speaking with God;

— continual meditation on the divine goodness and on the mysteries of the Faith, especially the Passion of Christ;

— frequent meditations to arouse oneself to the love of God;

— reference of thoughts, words, actions to God; — grave distress at the absence of Christ;

— observance of the Commandments and the evangelical counsels;

— ecstasies and raptures and/or other external signs, with which at times the Lord enriches his Servants!165.

The persons who lived close to Mother Rosa Gattorno could very easily realize that her heart was truly full of love for God. A whole series of external signs, such as those just indicated and others like them, were there to indicate with clarity and expressive force an exceptional charge of this love. It is fitting to give the word at once to the witnesses.

Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, witness V at the Roman Process, has brought out multiple habitual manifestations of the Servant of God's love for the Lord:

«During all the time that I was with her, I never noticed the slightest defect [...]. She vividly recommended to her sisters to avoid the smallest faults, because — she said — the devil does not begin with big things, he begins perhaps with a pin, and not only to her sisters did she make this recommendation, but especially at the novitiate where she went once or twice a week. When she heard of some grave offense against the Lord, she made a sign of horror, and expressed it with a trembling and made the sign of the cross on her forehead. ‘Let us pray — she said — for these sinners: we must make up with prayers for the failings of others’. The Servant of God was always in the presence of God and united with Jesus; and one may say that she never said a word without some ejaculatory prayer or some aspiration to Jesus in between. The devotions dear to her she sought to spread also among others, and she also inquired how they practiced this or that devotion and instructed them on the way to pray.

Speaking of God she was moved and could not hide her tears well [...]. During prayer she paid no heed to anyone»166.

With great clarity, Cardinal Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, who for so many years dealt intimately with the Servant of God, speaks to us of the divine charity that burned in her enamored heart:

«Most ardent was her love for God, toward whom she always took heed with every solicitude not to cause displeasure even by the slightest fault. Sometimes she told me in confidence that she found herself embarrassed in the search for faults to accuse to the confessor. By her charity she expiated with harsh penances her presumed faults and those of others, that the wrath of the Lord might be calmed.

In conversing with her I always had to note her great love for God, although she did nothing to manifest it to me, being always reserved in her words, in her behavior, in every act of hers. Such reserve was constant with everyone, and she made her hiddenness the continual object of her prayer, as she told me, so that no one could have known what flame of charity burned in her heart, had he not known the continuity of her acts and the results of her works.

Her charity toward God moved her to the prompt correction also of the defects of her religious. She did not spare measures necessary to avoid inconveniences, even if they were painful to her heart. Charity toward God made her afflicted when she came to know of grave faults of others.

Charity moved her to knock constantly at the Heart of God for her son and for the brother whom she knew far from God [...]. Her charity toward God moved her in the conferences to the religious; when she instructed them on prayer she exhorted them to regular discipline, interpreting successively all the points of the rule. In a word, God was the one who occupied her whole heart. God, however, to his faithful servant who loved him so much, made her heart ever more ardent toward Him. And she herself told me that it seemed to her sometimes that her heart swelled and her ribs dilated, and she felt obliged to beg the Lord to lessen somewhat for her the effects of those ardors toward Him. Ordinarily in the Servant of God nothing extraordinary was seen, as I have already said. Only, however, when she came out of her room after those extraordinary recollections in it for reasons of prayer and penances, I had occasion to notice her, and with me the other religious, pale in the face and swollen to such a degree, even in the hands, as to be unable to hold for some brief time even the pen to write»167.

59. — An ever very valid method for measuring the intensity of love for God is given by the effort made to avoid offending Him. Now, according to the testimonies already gathered and so many other depositions of witnesses who repeatedly speak of the hatred of sin, viscerally felt by the Servant of God, it is evident that Mother Rosa Gattorno, in this respect too, has left us further most abundant proofs of heroic charity. We gather in succession some of these testimonies.

Sr. Maria Teresa Patti di Sorrentino, witness VI at the Palermo Process, affirms:

«I saw the Servant of God work in every way to prevent mortal sin. She grieved immensely at the offense of God and on her face one could perceive the painful impression her heart received from it. I was never present at a blasphemy uttered in her presence; several times I saw her mark her forehead with her thumb in the sign of the cross when she heard of an offense done to God, or of some sinner; often she exclaimed: ‘My Jesus, mercy’. She continually recommended to her daughters to pray for the conversion of sinners and to appease divine justice.

The mother abhorred venial fault, and I always saw her use every spiritual means to remove or avoid even the least offense done to the Lord; this above all with her daughters. Many times I saw the Mother employ every means to lead back to the right path the strayed and the lukewarm. Particularly with her daughters she never failed to correct them and help them. To lead souls back to God was the principal aim of her life, and her charity was therefore exercised in hospitals, in orphanages, in prisons, in boarding schools, in homes, with the aim of skillfully directing souls to God»168

Sr. A. Fara Martinengo, witness XV at the Roman Process, adds:

«I never saw in her any imperfection. And she recommended to sisters and laypeople not only to watch so as to keep themselves immune from any fault but also exhorted them to abstain from certain things even though lawful in order to earn merits and acquire a higher degree of love of God. She exhorted us to the disinterested love of Jesus: ‘We must not — she told us — give to Him in order to have, but give and offer disinterestedly and out of pure love and gratitude’.

She was moved, even fell silent, when she heard blasphemies or other things offensive to God. ‘At these offenses — she said — if the Eternal Father were capable of weeping, He would weep tears of blood, as my soul weeps’. She exhorted us to procure reparation either by having a child pray, or a gravely ill person, or by seeking to take advantage of a good moment to raise, with some good word, a strayed soul to God. According to the qualities of the persons she made exhortations, that they might return to God, while God would then assist them in their needs in which they found themselves»169.

60. — Carried by her most ardent love of God, she worked tirelessly throughout her whole life so that her communities might be a fruitful garden of holiness in the respect for and fulfillment of the rules as an expression of consecration to the Lord in the Church. Thus, for example, Sr. A. Cunegonda Pacini, witness VI at the Naples Process, testifies:

«I have always admired the Servant of God for her life, most virtuous in every respect. She exercised herself greatly in mental prayer and in the practice of meditation. She cared greatly that the sisters should not miss it. She always said: ‘Whoever does not make meditation is not saved and does not persevere in the vocation’. She did not miss the common prayers and when she was prevented by reasons of her office she went afterwards to the chapel to make up for them and in that case always associated some other sister, since she said that prayers in common have great value before God. In private, moreover, it is well known in the community that the Servant of God withdrew for a long time in prayer, and that after lunch she went to the chapel where she remained long hours before Jesus in the Sacrament.

Her conversations were always inspired by holy things and things of God and even during recreation she always took topics from the life of some saint or also spoke of some virtue and of the way to exercise it. On every Sunday she wanted us to make acts of reparation to the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus; for this she had the Most Holy Sacrament exposed in our church and established adoration in turns of twelve sisters and she herself took part. Out of love for Jesus in the Sacrament and to make reparation for the outrages of sinners she made the other foundation of deaf-mute adoring sisters»170

9. Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, witness IX at the Roman Process, recalls:

«As to the charity of the Servant of God I am certain that she sought to avoid even the slightest defects. She greatly inculcated the observance of the rules, even in small things, because — she said — ‘the devil does not tempt in great things, but in small things, so as then to make his way to the great ones’. ‘When you have a little free time — she told us — instead of wasting time in idle words, go to Jesus, and be thieves. Steal, steal’. I would not know how to name the least defect I noticed in her. She suffered greatly if she saw silence not well observed; if she knew that in some community there was not perfect regular observance, she rebuked. Having learned that in one community there was not much recollection, by way of penance, as appears from a letter, she obliged them always to speak in a low voice for a week [...].

She felt horror of every sin. I myself heard her exclaim so many times: ‘By the grace of God no, no’; mortal sin has never entered her work, and of this I can hold my head high. Yes, it is true that some have transgressed, but the Holy Mother (Saint Anne) drove her out in time. If I knew that sin were entering the work of the Lord, I would die of grief»171.

Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, witness XX at the Roman Process, informs us further of Mother Rosa's exquisite care that even «the slightest venial fault» be avoided in her communities:

«I never discovered any defect in her; and she recommended to us to do all we could to avoid even the slightest venial fault. ‘As for mortal sin — she said, crossing her forehead — my God, I believe that in the houses of the Daughters of Saint Anne it will never happen’. In her conferences she explained to us sometimes how venial sin can be committed, and that it must be avoided, because it too is a great offense to the Lord. She grieved so much when she came to know that in one of our houses murmuring was not avoided, and to that sister who had murmured she said: ‘Take care, my daughter, before making communion try to go to confession’. And she also wanted her to ask pardon of the one of whom she had murmured. Sometimes it happened that some sister murmured without understanding that it was murmuring: then the Servant of God called her to herself, instructed her and made her understand how she had murmured and put her on guard. When she spoke of the Passion, I saw tears fall from her eyes; and when in the conferences, or speaking privately, her talk turned to the love of God, her face became a flame»172.

61. — Among the manifold manifestations of divine love with which the life and work of Mother Rosa are singularly enriched, one must highlight in the very first place piety, the true kind and by no means «devotional or sentimental piety, which interposes itself between the soul and God and takes from love that dynamic restlessness of one who lives not for himself but for God and for others»173. This piety, manifestation and fruit of divine love, informed the whole earthly existence of Mother Rosa to its ultimate consequences and its smallest details. So Fr. Iriarte expresses himself in this regard in his volume Fisionomia spirituale di Rosa Gattorno:

«The virginal heart, while succeeding in freeing the affective potential in order to polarize it in uncreated Love, increases the capacity to love all that God loves. Such polarization becomes all the more fruitful the more vital the union with the supreme Good. One of the first manifestations of true love, guided by faith, is piety, the true kind, not devotional or sentimental piety, which interposes itself between the soul and God and takes from love that dynamic restlessness of one who lives not for himself but for God and for others. Rosa Gattorno knew how to orient, at the crucial moment of her life, the richness of her affectivity so as to be able to develop an authentic piety centered on the fundamental contents of the faith: the God-Trinity, Jesus Christ, the Virgin Mary, some saints as models and protectors, the Church, the Institute, the spiritual daughters, the poor»174.

The authentic love of Mother Rosa, modeled on that of Christ, becomes with Him redemptive. So Fr. Iriarte speaks of it:

«The heart of Rosa Gattorno, a woman's heart, endowed with a rich sensitivity and an exceptional capacity for welcome and affective giving, was made to love. And it was also a heart made to suffer. Suffering enters into the Christian logic of oblative and redemptive love, since the love of God for us was manifested in the fact that He sent his Son as an expiatory victim for our sins (1 Jn 4:9f.); and the Son of God showed love for the Father and for men by submitting to the passion and to death on the cross. It is not only a matter of Mother Rosa's personal spirituality: to love and to suffer will also be her destiny as foundress and will constitute her central message to the Daughters of Saint Anne [...]. Rosa Gattorno belongs to the throng of so many great lovers who, like Saint Teresa of Avila, Saint John of the Cross, Saint Mary Magdalene de' Pazzi, Saint Veronica Giuliani, made of suffering, so to speak, the why of their existence: a mission, that is, to complete what is lacking in Christ's afflictions (cf. Col 1:24), collaborating in his redemptive immolation»175.

62. — When Mother Rosa speaks of the love of God to her daughters, her language becomes insistent and seems to burn. So she expresses herself in a letter to Caterina Rapallino:

«Caterina, my daughter, if you knew how much Jesus loves you you would surely be mad for Him and would do nothing else but clasp Him to your Heart and say to Him: ‘My love, speak to me, command me, for I will do everything that pleases you. Yes, my daughter, you will feel it if you follow his will and his voice, and you will see that He Himself with love will console you»176.

No theme is so pleasing to Mother Rosa as this of love. In a letter to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa she confesses:

«Ah, dear superior: I assure you that merely in writing these two lines that speak of charity, I feel in myself a strong desire and for what? My

p. 75

God, calm in me this why, which makes me suffer too much. Ah, when will that day come when I can give vent to so great a desire of mine? What am I doing? My superior, forgive me, but what do you want? When this thought seizes my mind, I cannot contain it»177.

63. — Nothing, therefore, produced in her such joy as giving pleasure to God, living a life of true, most ardent love, as she writes to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni:

«My daughter, if you knew what consolation I feel merely in pronouncing this word (‘to give pleasure to God’) and even more if the sweet thought of being or of being able to become his good pleasure awakens vividly in me, I feel wholly outside myself, so that if I had to face the cruelest martyrdom I would feel nothing; who can doubt it? Perhaps there is some creature who thinks differently and does not feel what I say? I do not believe it, but only if I knew that there were someone who experienced it more than I, I would weep and so much and with so much effort would I want to work to get ahead of her»178.

To the same Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni she manifested her greatest desire in regard to her loving relations with God:

«I desire one thing from you and it is that you try to study how to love God with a love wholly pure and ardent. If you arrive at this, I shall say to you: do what you will, said St. Augustine. Yes, my dear, love this dear God the Father, and you will do everything with pleasure»179.

4. Charity toward neighbor

64. — The range of charitable acts, gestures and behaviors of the Servant of God toward different social categories is very wide; one might say she was a fruitful and industrious seeker of needs to be met, of aid to be distributed, of miseries to be relieved. Mother Rosa was a specialist above all in care for the poor, the sick, the afflicted, and therefore it can well be said that charity toward neighbor was certainly her chief virtue. Its heroicity needs no discursive demonstration, so macroscopic does it appear in the informative sources, which illustrate with a wealth of concrete facts not only Mother Rosa's exceptional maternal charity for poor and abandoned childhood, but a whole vast range of works of mercy, material and spiritual, toward the most varied social categories: from orphans to poor widows, to priests, to girls, to sisters, to her own relatives, to friends and even to enemies.

It suffices to put together here, by way of example, a few among the many eyewitness testimonies.

65. — Sr. A.
